Bioinformatics for One Health Surveillance: AMR and Zoonotic Threats
summary: The field of bioinformatics has become a cornerstone of the One Health approach, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. In particular, the rapid advancement of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has transformed pathogen detection and surveillance, enabling high-resolution tracking of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes and zoonotic pathogens. However, translating large-scale genomic data into actionable insights requires integrative computational tools that can manage complexity across biological domains. The persistent rise of AMR and the increasing frequency of zoonotic spillover events underscore the need for advanced, cross-sectoral surveillance systems that unify diverse data sources to inform global health preparedness and policy.

title: Biomarker Discovery and Validation in Cognitive and Behavioral Neurology
summary: Recent advances in molecular biology, neuroimaging, and computational methods have accelerated the identification of biomarkers for cognitive and behavioral disorders. Biomarkers derived from cerebrospinal fluid, blood, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, or genetic and epigenetic signatures can improve early diagnosis, track disease progression, predict treatment response, and serve as clinical trial endpoints. However, the translation from biomarker discovery to clinical practice remains limited by challenges in reproducibility, standardization, validation across diverse populations, and regulatory acceptance.

title: Brain and Behavior in the Wild: Mobile Neuroimaging and Wearable Technologies
summary: Research in cognitive and behavioral neuroscience is increasingly shifting towards understanding how the brain operates in the dynamic contexts of everyday life. Traditionally, most knowledge about brain function has been derived from tightly controlled laboratory or clinical settings, which often fail to account for the complexity and richness of real-world environmental and social influences. Recent advancements highlight the limitations of these controlled paradigms for capturing the temporal and contextual variability that shapes cognition, emotion, and symptoms across the lifespan. While several studies have demonstrated the promise of mobile neuroimaging and wearable solutions, critical questions remain about their ability to provide ecologically valid, reliable, and clinically useful insights. title: Cognitive control in motion: How physical fitness supports cognition–movement coupling across the lifespan
summary: Cognition–movement coupling is an essential domain within cognitive neuroscience and movement science, examining how thought processes integrate with physical action to support adaptive behavior. In daily life, tasks such as navigating complex environments or responding to changing conditions rely heavily on the seamless interaction between cognitive control and motor coordination. Recent investigations have revealed that physical fitness may play a vital role in modulating this interaction. Evidence indicates that higher fitness is linked with improved executive function, gait stability, dual-task performance, and neural efficiency during motor activity. However, findings remain scattered across disciplines—ranging from psychology and neuroscience to biomechanics and rehabilitation—hindering a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms through which fitness influences cognition–movement dynamics. title: Current Perspectives of The Neurobiology of Prosody and Rhythm
summary: Prosody and rhythm are core components of speech that allow the brain to transform acoustic signals into linguistic and affective meaning. The interplay of pitch, stress, timing, and intonation patterns conveys syntactic structure, emotion, and communicative intent, while rhythmic organization supports segmentation, prediction, and motor coordination. Recent neuroscience research has revealed that prosodic and rhythmic functions depend on distributed neural networks spanning auditory, motor, subcortical, and cerebellar regions, coordinated by oscillatory activity across temporal scales. Despite these advances, key questions remain about how these systems develop, how their dysfunction contributes to communication disorders, and how prosody interacts with music, movement, and emotion across contexts and languages. Bridging these knowledge gaps is essential to understand how the brain encodes the temporal and melodic contours that shape human speech.

Infectious Diseases Associated with Reproductive Disorders in Animals
summary: Infectious biological agents are significant causes of reproductive disorders and thus are of high research priority in animal industries around the world. Reproductive failures can include infectious abortion which is of significant concern for veterinary health and economic losses to domestic species producers. These factors not only impact the prosperity of animal industry but are also important from public health point of view as many infectious agents harbor zoonotic potential. Bacterial, viral, parasites, protozoon, chlamydial and fungal infectious agents are known to have direct impact on reproductive health of animal, making identification and diagnosis critical.

title: Innovative Approaches in Glioma Therapy: Exploring New Therapeutic Frontiers- Volume III
summary: Gliomas remain some of the most formidable and heterogeneous tumors of the central nervous system, classified as astrocytic, oligodendroglial, and ependymal neoplasms with World Health Organization (WHO) grades I–IV. Despite advancement in surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, outcomes—particularly for glioblastoma (grade IV glioma)—remain dismal, with median overall survival rarely exceeding 15 months. Resistance to conventional therapy, high rates of recurrence, and the inability of most therapeutic agents to cross the blood–brain barrier continue to pose major challenges, driving the need for novel, targeted treatment strategies with greater efficacy and lower toxicity.

title: Molecular mechanisms of Tau and TDP-43 pathology, and interaction of co-pathology in neurodegenerative disease
summary: Neurodegeneration research has increasingly recognized the pivotal contributions of specific proteinopathies to cognitive decline and behavioral alterations seen with aging. Among these, transactive response DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) and tau have emerged as central players in conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. While tauopathies and TDP-43 proteinopathies were initially considered largely distinct, growing evidence reveals overlapping distribution patterns, synergistic interactions, and converging mechanisms underlying their accumulation in vulnerable neuronal populations. This complexity has sparked debate regarding their relative contributions to neurodegenerative phenotypes, the sequence of their pathological events, and the reasons for their frequent comorbidity, especially in older individuals.

title: Quantum theory, biological organization, and the mind-brain problem
summary: The relationship between physical theory and biological organization remains one of the most challenging in contemporary science. Part of the inspiration of this topic comes from the intellectual legacy of Erwin Schrödinger, especially the questions raised in What is Life? and Mind and Matter, as well as from the centenary of wave mechanics. Schrödinger’s reflections helped shape enduring discussions on order, information, stability, and the organization of living matter. Today, these themes continue to resonate in debates on biological information, neural complexity, memory, brain dynamics, and the conceptual relation between mind and brain. Rather than treating these questions as purely historical, this Research Topic approaches them as still-active problems at the intersection of theoretical physics, life sciences, and neuroscience.

title: Screens and the Developing Mind: Digital Technology, Mental Health, and Wellbeing in Children and Adolescents
summary: Digital technology and the pervasiveness of screens have become defining features of modern childhood and adolescence. Over the past two decades, smartphones, tablets, streaming media, video games, and social platforms have transformed how young people learn, communicate, and play. While these tools enhance educational opportunities and global connectivity, their pervasive presence has prompted urgent questions about their influence on mental health and neurodevelopment. Current evidence paints a complex picture—some studies reveal associations between excessive screen exposure and disruptions to sleep, emotion regulation, attention, and social interaction, while others highlight potential cognitive, creative, and therapeutic benefits depending on context, content, and usage patterns. Amid ongoing debates, the need persists for a comprehensive understanding of how digital environments intersect with developmental, psychological, and social processes.

title: Talk, Text, Connect: Naturalistic language and social meaning across brains and AI models
summary: For decades, cognitive neuroscience relied on highly controlled, albeit artificial, experimental designs using isolated words or fragmented sentences to map the linguistic brain. However, language in the real world is rarely static; it is a dynamic, social, and continuous medium used to build connection and convey complex intent. The recent "naturalistic turn" in neuroscience—utilizing stories, movies, and spontaneous dialogue—has revealed that the brain processes language through widespread, interconnected networks that are deeply sensitive to social context. Simultaneously, the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has provided researchers with unprecedented computational tools to simulate and predict human-like text processing. Despite these advancements, a significant gap remains in understanding how "social meaning"—the nuanced subtext and interpersonal resonance of communication—is represented across biological and artificial systems. title: α-Synuclein Propagation, Staging, and Disease Progression in Parkinson’s Disease and Related Synucleinopathies
summary: Misfolding and aggregation of α-synuclein are central pathological features of Parkinson’s disease and related synucleinopathies. While these proteinopathies have been intensively studied, effective disease-modifying therapies remain elusive. Recent work suggests that α-synuclein can adopt different forms (including conformers or putative strains), and that some synucleinopathies, especially rapidly progressing types, may involve α-synuclein species with higher aggregation, seeding, and propagation potential. These findings continue to shape debates on the molecular basis of disease progression and the clinical significance of biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis, and staging. However, important gaps remain in linking molecular events to clinical outcomes, and in understanding how aging-related factors influence the initiation, spread, and clearance of pathogenic α-synuclein. More direct links to clinically meaningful outcomes are needed to support translation and inform targeted therap
image_alt: α-Synuclein Propagation, Staging, and Disease Progression in Parkinson’s Disease and Related Synucleinopathies

title: Brain-computer interfaces for monitoring pain, fatigue, chronic disease and everyday well-being
summary: Pain, fatigue, and chronic disease represent some of the most prevalent and debilitating challenges in modern healthcare, yet their subjective and fluctuating nature makes them notoriously difficult to objectively assess and monitor. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising avenue for bridging this gap, enabling the continuous, non-invasive monitoring of neural and physiological correlates associated with these conditions. BCIs have the potential to transform how we understand, manage, and respond to pain, fatigue, and chronic illness in both clinical and everyday settings.

title: Evidence Based Treatments for Autism Spectrum Disorders
summary: Treatment for Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have evolved with the refined definition of ASD, identification of common co-morbidities, availability of ASD measurements and genetic typing. Despite this progress, existing challenges persist regarding the quality and clinical relevance of various interventions. Only two drugs have been FDA approved for ASD, namely Aripiprazole and Risperidone, both of which are prescribed for the management of irritability, which is considered a co-morbidity, lying outside of ASD core symptoms. Likewise, in many other parts of the world, the majority of medications prescribed for individuals with ASD target associated challenges such as irritability, aggression, hyperactivity, anxiety, sleep disturbances, and mood disorders, while the core symptoms of ASD (deficits in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive behaviors) remain largely unaddressed by existing pharmacotherapy. title: From Sound to Silence: Hearing Loss, Dementia, and the Search for Preventive and Restorative Therapies
summary: The global rise in life expectancy has brought with it a dramatic increase in age-related health conditions, particularly those affecting sensory and cognitive function. Among these, hearing loss and dementia are two of the most prevalent and interlinked challenges facing older adults. Recent studies increasingly suggest that hearing loss may not only precede dementia but could act as a modifiable risk factor for its onset and progression. Understanding this connection is crucial for developing early interventions that preserve cognitive health and overall quality of life in aging populations.

title: Neural Mechanisms, Computational Models, and Neurorehabilitation in Visual Processing Disorders
summary: Vision arises from the sophisticated processing of information along the retinocortical pathway. Disruptions to this neural circuitry, due to developmental anomalies, injury, or disease, lead to diverse visual processing disorders such as amblyopia and cortical visual impairment. Understanding these conditions necessitates a multidisciplinary approach integrating neuroscience, computation, and clinical practice. While advances in neuroimaging and computational modeling have deepened insights into neural mechanisms, and novel interventions like perceptual learning show rehabilitative promise, a significant gap remains in synthesizing these perspectives into a unified framework for diagnosis and treatment. This Research Topic aims to address this integrative challenge.

title: Neuromelanin and Iron in Parkinson's Disease: Mechanisms, Heterogeneity, Biomarkers, and Progression
summary: Understanding the intricate interplay between neuromelanin and iron in the brain is a rapidly evolving area of Parkinson’s disease (PD) research. Parkinson’s disease is characterized by extensive heterogeneity in both clinical presentation and disease progression, a variability that is only partially explained by traditional pathological markers. Recent advances highlight that neuromelanin, a pigmented polymer in dopaminergic neurons, and brain iron content, particularly within the substantia nigra and related brainstem nuclei, may jointly modulate neurodegeneration and underlie the observed clinical diversity. However, despite mounting evidence linking regional differences in neuromelanin and iron with distinct PD subtypes and trajectories, significant gaps remain in comprehending the mechanisms driving these variations, how they interact at the molecular and network levels, and their implications for precision diagnostics.
image_alt: Neuromelanin and Iron in Parkinson's Disease: Mechanisms, Heterogeneity, Biomarkers, and Progression

title: Neuromuscular ageing: neural drivers of sarcopenia and functional decline
summary: Sarcopenia is a major feature of ageing and is characterized by a progressive decline in skeletal muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity. While traditionally viewed as a muscle-centered disorder, accumulating evidence indicates that age-related alterations of the nervous system play a critical role in its development and progression. Structural and functional changes in the central nervous system, degeneration of motor neurons, remodeling of motor units, and impairment of neuromuscular junctions contribute to reduced neural drive and compromised muscle activation. In addition, altered sensorimotor integration, neuroinflammation, and neurodegenerative processes further amplify neuromuscular dysfunction. Understanding sarcopenia as a neuromuscular disorder underscores the need to investigate neural ageing as a key determinant of muscle decline and functional impairment in older adults.

title: Personality, Emotion Regulation, and The Dynamics of Aggression in Social Behavior
summary: Aggression remains a central focus in personality and social psychology due to its far-reaching implications for interpersonal relationships, mental health, and societal wellbeing. Despite decades of research, the field continues to grapple with understanding the intricate ways in which personality traits, affective dynamics, and situational influences converge to give rise to aggressive behavior. Foundational models have pinpointed trait impulsivity, antagonism, and callous unemotional characteristics as robust individual predictors of aggression, while recent investigations underscore the importance of self-regulatory capacities such as emotion regulation in moderating these effects. Large-scale empirical studies and integrative theoretical frameworks have increasingly moved beyond viewing aggression as a simple behavioral response, instead conceptualizing it as a product of continuous interaction among personality systems, emotional states, and social environments. title: Spinal Degeneration, Deformity, and Spinal Cord Injury
summary: Spine disorders represent a crucial intersection of musculoskeletal and neurological pathology, with spinal degeneration, deformity, and spinal cord injury forming an interlinked triad that poses persistent clinical and research challenges. Historically, each element—degeneration, deformity, and cord injury—has been considered predominantly in isolation, resulting in compartmentalized approaches to research, diagnosis, and therapy. Recent studies, however, have begun to reveal that these conditions share overlapping and mutually reinforcing pathophysiological mechanisms: degeneration may foster instability and deformity, while these structural changes in turn precipitate spinal cord compromise and neurological deficits. Spinal cord injuries can then further drive instability and degenerative processes, perpetuating a self-amplifying cycle that underlies progressively worsening morbidity. Despite mounting evidence of such bidirectional interactions, major gaps remain in our coordinated

title: The Intricate Interplay Between Stressors and Memory: Experimental, Theoretical, and Non-Canonical Perspective
summary: Stress and memory research continues to uncover the intricate and often paradoxical ways in which stressors influence memory processes. While numerous studies highlight how stress-related hormones can enhance memory consolidation yet impair retrieval, the underlying evolutionary and adaptive roles of these mechanisms remain somewhat elusive. This field's complexity is amplified by the cross-species insights into these processes and the varied outcomes dependent on factors such as stress intensity, memory phase, and learning context. Despite progress in understanding neuromodulators' roles in emotional memory, there is still a considerable challenge in predicting a memory's outcome—whether it will be strengthened, weakened, or inhibited—following a stressful event.

title: Unraveling the Neuropsychological Ground of Substance-Related and Non-Substance-Related Addictive Behaviors
summary: Modern neuropsychology views addiction as the behavioral consequence of neuroadaptation including notably maladaptive recalibration of the reward system from "liking" (hedonic pleasure) to "wanting" (compulsive craving), a breakdown in executive control and abnormal emotional processing. The state of the art in addiction neuropsychology has shifted from a simple "dopamine rush" theory to a complex neuro-circuitry model characterized by multiple structural and functional brain reorganization. Neuropsychology considers both the risk factors and the consequences of addictive behaviors, with an interest on recovery and the reversibility of neurobiological process. Based on the heterogeneity of profiles, the field is moving toward individual neuropsychological phenotyping, including cognitive, behavioral and emotional abilities, which would allow us to stratify patients and provide personalized and adapted care.

title: eDNA to Ecosystem Decisions: Molecular Biodiversity Monitoring Integrated with Forecast Models
summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) and metabarcoding are transforming the field of biodiversity monitoring, enabling scientists to infer species presence, community composition, and ecological patterns from trace genetic material in environmental samples. These molecular approaches provide high sensitivity and broad taxonomic coverage, often outperforming conventional survey methods in detecting elusive, rare, invasive, or cryptic species across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems. Recent advances in sequencing and bioinformatics have expanded their potential for real-time biodiversity assessment. However, key challenges persist in connecting raw molecular detections to ecological meaning, specifically, in translating eDNA data into measures of species abundance, functional diversity, and ecosystem processes. Current studies increasingly highlight both the power and the limitations of eDNA signals in capturing ecological complexity, revealing an urgent need for integrative frameworks
image_alt: eDNA to Ecosystem Decisions: Molecular Biodiversity Monitoring Integrated with Forecast Models

title: Biomaterials for Neural Repair in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Mechanisms, Interfaces, and Translational Advances
summary: The progressive loss of neuronal structure and function in disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) remains one of the greatest challenges in modern neuroscience. The emergence of biocompatible and bioactive materials - including hydrogels, nanocomposites, and carbon-based scaffolds - now offers powerful tools to support neural regeneration and neuroprotection in these conditions.

title: Botulinum Neurotoxins in the Management of Movement Disorders: Clinical and Therapeutic Innovations
summary: Botulinum neurotoxins (BoNT) have become a cornerstone in the treatment of hyperkinetic movement disorders, offering targeted and reversible chemodenervation that has significantly improved patient outcomes. Over recent decades, the use of BoNT has evolved beyond its initial indications for cervical dystonia and blepharospasm, now encompassing hemifacial spasm, oromandibular dystonia, sialorrhea, limb dystonias, tremor, muscle hypertonia in Parkinsonism, and select functional and cerebellar syndromes. Technological advances such as ultrasound, electromyography (EMG), and kinematic guidance have increased precision in targeting affected muscles, while new serotypes and formulation sciences expand therapeutic possibilities. Despite these developments, there remains considerable heterogeneity in outcomes, largely attributable to variation in patient phenotypes, targeting methodologies, and inconsistencies in outcome assessment. title: Exploring the Intersection of Depression and Alzheimer’s: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Strategies
summary: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder, most notably associated with memory deficits and cognitive impairment. Despite extensive research, there remains an urgent need to develop disease-modifying therapies that may slow the progression of AD. Late-life depression has emerged as a significant risk factor for AD. Genome-wide association studies have indicated that the genetic risk for depression may contribute to the development of AD, whereas AD genetic risk does not reciprocally increase the risk of depression. Shared molecular features between AD and depression, such as disturbances in cholinergic/serotonergic neurotransmission and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, warrant further exploration.

title: Harnessing Reproductive Diversity and Technology for Wildlife Conservation Success
summary: Reproductive science plays a critical role in wildlife conservation, offering innovative tools to counteract pressures such as genetic erosion, habitat fragmentation, and altered reproductive patterns across animal taxa. Emerging research highlights how species-specific reproductive strategies—including unique mechanisms of ovulation, seasonal breeding adaptations, and reproductive senescence—fundamentally shape population resilience and determine the feasibility of interventions. While considerable progress has been achieved through both fundamental and applied studies, much remains to be learned about how reproductive diversity mediates survival, adaptive potential, and long-term sustainability of wildlife populations, especially under mounting environmental and anthropogenic stressors. Advances in assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs), biobanking, and non-invasive monitoring have catalyzed conservation breakthroughs, yet gaps persist regarding their standardization and applicabi

title: Multiscale Modeling of Brain Function
summary: The human brain is a quintessentially multiscale system, characterized by a complex hierarchy of interactions spanning several orders of magnitude in both space and time. From the rapid dynamics of ion channels and synaptic transmission at the molecular level to the integrated activity of microcircuits and large-scale cortical networks, brain function emerges through the orchestration of these disparate scales. Historically, computational models have often focused on a single level of abstraction, either detailed biophysical simulations or simplified top-down phenomenological models. However, it is increasingly recognized that understanding cognitive phenomena such as memory, perception, and the progression of neurological disorders requires a more holistic approach. Bridging the gap between microscopic mechanisms and macroscopic behavior remains one of the most formidable challenges in neuroscience. To truly decode how the brain processes information, we must develop robust frameworks

title: Occupational Stress, Mental Health, and Resilience in the Veterinary Workforce
summary: Veterinary professionals work in emotionally and ethically demanding environments, often under substantial time and workload pressure. Growing international evidence points to high levels of burnout, psychological distress, compassion fatigue, and suicidal ideation across the veterinary workforce. These outcomes are linked to multiple occupational stressors, including long and irregular working hours, challenging client interactions, financial pressures, and moral distress related to animal welfare and end-of-life decisions.

title: Recent Advances in Bovine Tuberculosis - Volume II
summary: Bovine tuberculosis (bTB) is a zoonotic disease caused by Mycobacterium bovis and other members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. These bacteria, together with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the etiological agent of human TB, are responsible for a similar pulmonary disease. M. bovis can be transmitted from livestock like cattle to humans through the consumption of unpasteurized milk and derivatives. Furthermore, this pathogen is a potential risk to workers in close contact with infected animals, especially in slaughterhouses. The impact of bTB in the meat and dairy industries results in serious economical losses. As a zoonotic disease and a human health hazard, bTB is considered a One Health issue.
image_alt: Recent Advances in Bovine Tuberculosis - Volume II

title: Timing the senses: From auditory temporal coherence to audiovisual integration
summary: Human perception operates within a chaotic sensory environment, where the brain must constantly determine which signals arise from the same source. A critical mechanism for this is temporal coherence, being the degree to which different sensory features fluctuate together over time. In the auditory domain, temporal coherence is a primary driver for stream segregation, allowing the brain to bind diverse frequencies into a single "object." However, this principle extends beyond audition. Temporal structure serves as a fundamental organizing principle for perception across sensory modalities, acting as a "glue" that helps the brain determine which signals belong together. While we understand that timing is important for both auditory grouping and multisensory binding, the precise transition from intramodal temporal coherence to intermodal audiovisual integration remains a complex challenge in human neuroscience.

Epileptogenesis, the process by which an initially non-epileptic brain becomes capable of generating recurrent spontaneous seizures, remains incompletely understood. Post-traumatic epileptogenesis (PTE) involves a dynamic interplay of molecular, cellular, and circuit-level changes, including synaptic reorganization, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and maladaptive plasticity of inhibitory and excitatory networks.

title: Targeting Cognition and Brain Health in Neurodegenerative Diseases through Nutraceuticals
summary: Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, pose significant challenges to global public health, affecting cognitive processes and featuring a progressive decline of several brain functions. The search for effective interventions is ongoing, with recent focus turning towards the potential benefits of food supplements and nutraceuticals on cognitive functions and brain health due to their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuromodulatory properties. Emerging research suggests these dietary additions might influence the physiopathogenic processes underlying brain health, cognitive aging, and neurodegenerative diseases, potentially offering neuroprotection and symptom management. However, the diversity in compounds, varied mechanisms of action, and the inconsistency in clinical trials underline the complexity of their effectiveness.

summary: Modern neuroscience has transitioned from small-scale manual observations to a data-intensive field powered by computational innovation. Traditionally focused on the biological structures and physiological functions of neural circuits, the discipline now increasingly relies on computer modeling, large-scale data analysis, and AI-driven diagnostics. This interdisciplinary shift blends biology and chemistry with computer science and engineering, transforming processes like neural circuit mapping, which once took months, into high-speed operations via deep learning.

title: The Third Dimension of Urban Ecology: Biological Processes and Adaptation in High-Density Environments
summary: The accelerating trends of global warming and urbanization pose significant challenges to the ecological resilience, human thermal comfort, and survival of organisms in high-density cities. Urban areas represent highly complex three-dimensional systems, where thermal exposure, energy exchange, and biological responses occur across both horizontal and vertical dimensions. Vegetation canopies, building facades, street canyon spaces, and ground habitats collectively form a three-dimensional urban thermal landscape, shaping microclimate patterns and adaptive spaces for organisms. In this context, the “third dimension” of urban ecology focuses on three-dimensional spatial structures, using high-precision acquisition technologies such as LiDAR and 3D reconstruction to build digital 3D scenarios, and analyzing the core role of 3D structures in mitigating thermal stress in response to climate challenges.

title: Advancing Health Equity and Wellbeing for Migrants and Refugees in the Global North
summary: International migration and displacement are defining features of the 21st century, shaping societies and transforming public health landscapes worldwide. Migrant and refugee populations enrich destination communities culturally and economically, but also face unique and persistent challenges ranging from mental health stressors and social inequalities to work-related injury and various barriers to care. As global crises, economics, and policy shifts intensify the flow of migrants and refugees to countries in the Global North, understanding and addressing the health needs of these populations is more urgent than ever. The purpose of this collection is to spark multidisciplinary dialogue and novel research on the health determinants, outcomes, and interventions critical to promoting health equity and wellbeing for migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers.

title: Buddhist Contemplative Practices Meet Positive Psychology: A Pathway to Enhanced Well-being
summary: The intersection of contemplative science and positive psychology has garnered increasing attention as scholars and practitioners seek integrative approaches to mental health and well-being. Buddhist traditions, with their deep-rooted contemplative frameworks, have long emphasized awareness, compassion, and self-transcendence as paths to liberation from suffering. In parallel, positive psychology has advanced the scientific study of happiness, flourishing, and character strengths, focusing on cultivating human potential. Recent research has highlighted how Buddhist contemplative practices—such as mindfulness, loving-kindness (metta), and compassion meditation—can complement positive psychology’s theoretical foundations by offering empirically supported means of fostering prosocial emotions, resilience, and self-regulation. Yet, despite growing interest, significant gaps remain in systematically bridging these two paradigms. Theoretical integration is still in its infancy, and empirical

title: Deep Learning for High-Dimensional Sense, Non-Linear Signal Processing and Intelligent Diagnosis, vol III
summary: This is a Volume 3 of our ( Volume 1 and Volume 2 ). Accurate interpretation of complex, high-dimensional signals derived from diagnostic tools such as EEG and MRI is crucial for advancing the understanding and treatment of mental health disorders. These signals, characterized by their high dimensionality, non-linearity, and low signal-to-noise ratios, pose significant challenges in terms of analysis and practical application. However, with the burgeoning field of medical big data and the advances in deep learning technologies, unprecedented opportunities emerge for enhancing real-time diagnostic and monitoring systems within psychiatric settings. This landscape calls for innovative approaches in integrating IoT with psychiatric practices to revolutionize how we detect, monitor, and treat mental health conditions.

title: Mechanisms and Effects of Music Education on Learning and Wellbeing in Childhood and Adolescence
summary: Music education has emerged as a promising and accessible component of school curricula, studied for its potential to enhance children’s development and wellbeing. Recent advances—spurred by large-scale initiatives such as the WHO-commissioned review by Fancourt and Finn (2019)—have integrated epidemiological findings, classroom-based interventions, and mechanistic research. The field now benefits from neuroimaging, psychobiological, and longitudinal evidence demonstrating how structured musical activities in educational settings may influence cognitive maturation, stress regulation, academic performance, and emotional functioning across childhood and adolescence.

summary: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly used in cybersecurity to support threat detection, incident response, anomaly identification, and adaptive defense. While many AI-driven methods report strong results in benchmark datasets and controlled experimental settings, their translation into operational cybersecurity environments remains limited. In practice, deployed systems must function under changing traffic patterns, incomplete and noisy observations, heterogeneous infrastructures, limited computational resources, and strict latency requirements. These conditions often expose a gap between experimental performance and operational reliability.

title: The Influence of Spiritual and Religious Practices on Mental Health and Psychological Resilience
summary: Within the field of health psychology, there is growing recognition of the importance of psychosocial factors such as spirituality and religiousness (S/R) in shaping mental health outcomes. Despite a longstanding debate, recent evidence points toward both beneficial and adverse effects of S/R practices on psychological well-being. Some studies highlight how spiritual or religious engagement can provide individuals with meaning, purpose, and feelings of belonging, which serve as protective factors against mood disorders and psychological distress. Conversely, other research points to potentially negative consequences arising from rigid belief systems, religious struggles, or experiences of exclusion and existential doubt. The complex relationship between S/R and mental health is further complicated by cultural, contextual, and individual differences, underscoring the need for more nuanced and integrative research in this area.

title: The bio-digital nexus: Exploring the fusion of biological neural networks and artificial intelligence
summary: For decades, neuroscience and artificial intelligence (AI) have shared a symbiotic history, with biological neural networks (BNNs) serving as the foundational blueprint for early computational models. While AI has since evolved into a powerhouse of data processing and pattern recognition, it often lacks the energy efficiency, plastic adaptability, and high-level generalization inherent in biological systems. Conversely, the complexity of the living brain presents a challenge that traditional analytical methods struggle to unravel. With all of this, today, we have entered the "Bio-Digital Nexus," a frontier where the boundaries between carbon-based cognition and silicon-based computation are increasingly blurred. Advances in neuroengineering, high-resolution neural recording, and deep learning now allow us to not only simulate biological processes but to directly interface artificial systems with living tissue. title: Developments in Animal Health Surveillance, volume III
summary: Animal health surveillance aims to facilitate early detection of outbreaks, disease control, animal welfare management, protection of public health, planning and decision-making. It is a continuous process of collecting key information to produce surveillance insights that are acted upon. The ongoing gathering of information is mostly based on the reporting of signs of disease by those close to animals such as animal owners, animal carers, animal health practitioners and diagnosticians. This is often complemented by regular diagnostic testing, in one form or another, to determine the health status of a particular animal population. This surveillance approach faces growing challenges in many countries worldwide. The challenges include the emergence of new pathogens, budget constraints, expansion of disease-vector ranges due to climate change, the spread of zoonoses as well as changing public and stakeholder expectations.

title: NeuroAI and the brain: Integrating brain-inspired computational models and large-scale AI architectures with computational theories of neural function
summary: The rapid ascent of large-scale artificial intelligence has provided neuroscience with a new set of powerful tools for modeling complex cognitive functions. Historically, computational neuroscience has balanced between biophysically detailed models of single neurons and abstract, small-scale circuit motifs. However, the ability of modern AI to perform human-like tasks in sensory processing, motor control, and linguistics offers a "top-down" framework to understand how the brain might organize high-dimensional data. This convergence, known as NeuroAI, suggests that the representational spaces of deep networks can serve as predictive scaffolds for neural activity. Despite this potential, a critical gap remains: most AI models lack the biological constraints, metabolic efficiency, and architectural diversity of the brain, while many neural models struggle to scale to the complexity of real-world behavior.

title: Commensal Bacteria as the Reservoir of Antimicrobial Resistance Genes
summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is widely recognized as a major global health threat, yet its ecological foundations remain insufficiently explored. While clinical pathogens are the primary focus of surveillance efforts, increasing evidence highlights the critical role of commensal bacteria as reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). This silent reservoir plays a critical role in the evolution and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), often preceding its emergence in clinically relevant pathogens. These microorganisms, which inhabit humans, animals, and environmental niches, constitute a vast and dynamic resistome that can be mobilized under selective pressure. Through mechanisms such as horizontal gene transfer mediated by plasmids, transposons, bacteriophages and outer membrane vesicles (OMV), commensals contribute to the emergence and dissemination of resistance traits across ecological boundaries. The characterization of genetic diversity, mapping of genes responsible for economically important traits, and the development of high-throughput genomic tools now underpin efforts to optimize animal performance, health, and resilience. summary: The field of trauma and disaster psychology has increasingly emphasized post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) as one of the most critical and enduring mental health outcomes of natural catastrophes such as earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, and wildfires. These events profoundly disrupt lives and communities, often resulting in both immediate and long-term emotional distress that spans generations. As natural disasters become more frequent and severe due to climate change, there is growing recognition that trauma are not confined to any specific age group — children, adolescents, adults, and older individuals are all affected in unique yet interconnected ways. While humanitarian efforts often prioritize physical safety and reconstruction, mental health recovery remains under-addressed, calling for a more holistic approach to post-disaster care and research.

title: Beyond the "Gold Standard": Improvements and Advancements in Autism Diagnosis
summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) continues to be one of the most intricate and diverse neurodevelopmental disorders, exhibiting considerable diversity among individuals and settings. Despite the use of "gold-standard" diagnostic tools like the ADOS-2, current diagnostic methods face several challenges; such as false negatives, issues with ecological validity and difficulties in diagnosis in individuals with comorbid conditions. Alongside this, additional factors such as masking and camouflaging confound the clinical picture, sometimes obscuring symptoms until later in life. However, diagnostic methods specifically tailored for adults remain more limited compared to the established tools available for children. To improve the accuracy and timeliness of diagnoses, it is crucial to address these diagnostic limitations.

title: Sepsis-Associated Encephalopathy as a Target for Neurological Biomarker Discovery
summary: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a pervasive complication of systemic infection, marked by acute disturbances in brain function without direct central nervous system infection. Despite its frequency and significant association with higher mortality, prolonged intensive care stays, and persistent neurocognitive impairment, the diagnosis of SAE remains challenging. Current clinical approaches rely largely on non-specific bedside neurological assessments, routine EEG, and standard neuroimaging, none of which offer definitive diagnostic power. As research efforts intensify, there is growing recognition of SAE’s heterogeneous pathogenesis, involving immune, metabolic, and microcirculatory mechanisms; yet, a lack of reliable, validated biomarkers continues to hinder progress in understanding, diagnosing, and treating this syndrome.

summary: The field of One Health is fundamentally concerned with the interconnectedness of human, animal, and ecosystem health and the challenges inherent in building systems that address threats spanning these domains. Despite wide endorsement of the One Health paradigm, there remain notable gaps in its operationalisation—particularly in efforts to build sustained, adaptable, and collaborative capacity across sectors. Current research highlights persistent obstacles related to siloed training, inconsistent governance arrangements, and insufficient mechanisms for cross-sectoral learning and resource mobilisation. Although promising models and institutional innovations have emerged, questions endure regarding how best to equip workforces, institutions, and communities to respond pre-emptively and adaptively to health challenges at this complex interface.

title: Advancing Translational Research in Brain-Heart Axis Interaction
summary: The field of neurocardiology explores the intricate, bidirectional communications between the brain and the heart-collectively termed the Brain-Heart Axis. This multifaceted network encompasses neural, autonomic, endocrine, immune, and metabolic signaling pathways responsible for maintaining physiological balance. Recent advances underscore that disruptions in the brain-heart axis can significantly contribute to a spectrum of disorders such as autonomic cardiomyopathy, neurodegenerative disease-linked cardiac complications, stroke, and stress-related cardiomyopathies. Despite considerable mechanistic insights into the neurocardiac interface, key questions remain regarding the translation of these findings to clinical practice, the full repertoire of signaling networks involved, and the development of specific biomarkers and targeted interventions.

title: Cognitive–motor interactions in aging: neural mechanisms, behavioral signatures, and functional consequences
summary: The fields of motor control and cognitive psychology have been traditionally separate, but research has fundamentally reshaped this distinction. We now understand that motor control and cognitive functions are inextricably linked, sharing neural pathways and competing for limited resources, especially in aging. As neural efficiency declines in aging, there is a tradeoff between using resources to support motor performance and cognitive function. For example, older adults often display reduced performance on complex tasks due to cognitive-motor interference, compared to younger adults. Understanding the mechanisms behind this shift is critical for distinguishing between healthy aging and early-stage neurodegeneration. It will also facilitate the development of interventions aimed at preserving functional independence.

summary: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a standard of care in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease and other movement disorders, such as dystonia and essential tremor, by offering improved and long-lasting symptom control where medical therapies prove insufficient. Increasingly, DBS is also used in epilepsy, where it offers a complementary clinical and mechanistic lens on how targeted stimulation modulates pathological brain networks. The growing ability to chronically sense and record neural activity in real-world settings, together with emerging adaptive “on-demand” stimulation paradigms, has transformed DBS from a therapeutic intervention into a tool for interrogating circuit dysfunction across disorders. title: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics of Tumor-Associated Microbiomes
summary: Tumors are complex ecosystems where cancer cells, stromal components, immune populations, and diverse microbial communities co-exist and co-evolve. Emerging evidence shows that bacteria, fungi, viruses, and other microorganisms colonizing primary and metastatic tumors can shape local immunity, metabolic landscapes, genomic instability, and clinical outcomes. These tumor-associated microbiomes are not passive passengers: they may influence carcinogenesis, progression, and response to chemo-, radio-, targeted, and immuno-therapies across both human and veterinary oncology. Yet, we still lack an integrative understanding of how ecological principles and evolutionary forces structure microbial communities within tumors, how these communities adapt to therapeutic perturbations, and how host genetics, tissue niches, and environmental exposures jointly shape tumor–microbe interactions. summary: The idea of ecological security, where large-scale environmental impacts are communicated as a threat to functioning ecosystems and human systems, has been around for many decades. Likewise, as ecological disturbances that may lead to substantial disruption to, or even collapse of, an ecosystem are being framed more often as ecological disasters that may have long-term and far-reaching impacts. While there are arguments on both sides for the characterization of ecological disturbances as threats or even disasters, the study of the resilience of ecosystems, species, or populations of plants and animals to large-scale changes, is a growing field in the backdrop the climate change and rapid environmental change.

These systems are central to domains such as healthcare, robotics, transportation, and smart infrastructure, where they interact with and control complex physical processes through integrated cyber-physical architectures. Supported by cloud-based technologies, autonomous systems can scale effectively, coordinate actions across distributed environments, and process massive volumes of data in real time. However, as adoption accelerates, new challenges arise in ensuring that such systems behave in ways that are safe, reliable, and aligned with human and societal intentions. The unpredictability of data-driven models, the opacity of deep learning systems, and the increasing interconnectedness of AI-driven applications demand new strategies to build confidence and trust in their operation.

title: Exploring the Hidden Diversity of Eukaryotic Microorganisms
summary: Eukaryotic microorganisms, or protists, are essential ecological agents that populate various environments like aquatic and soil systems. These organisms vary widely from autotrophs, which contribute fundamentally to primary production, to heterotrophs that act as vital intermediaries in food webs. While traditional morphological identification has been helpful, the integration of environmental DNA and modern molecular techniques such as metabarcoding has significantly expanded our understanding of the vast diversity and distribution of these microorganisms. Yet, despite advancements, a large segment of microbial diversity remains uncharacterized, posing a challenge to our understanding of protist evolution and their roles in ecosystems.

title: Future of Environmental Psychology
summary: Environmental psychology is an interdisciplinary field that examines the dynamic relationships between individuals, communities, and their physical, social, and ecological surroundings. Historically, the field has provided crucial insights into how people perceive, experience, and interact with built and natural environments, informing place-based experiences and guiding interventions aimed at promoting pro-environmental behavior, health, and wellbeing. As the scale and complexity of environmental challenges intensify, driven by rapid urbanization, climate change, biodiversity loss, as well as environmental experiences shaped by technology, the field faces a new set of questions and responsibilities. There is a growing need to understand how people interpret environmental risks, what makes environmental warnings actionable and trusted, and how social ties, trust, and communication shape individual and collective responses and resilience, particularly in times of crisis. Because gait reflects integrated motor, cognitive, and affective processes, it provides a promising behavioral window into clinically relevant alterations in psychiatric conditions.

As digital technology becomes more integrated into healthcare delivery, addressing disparities and ensuring equitable access to digital health solutions is paramount. Despite the potential for digital health to bridge existing healthcare gaps, many solutions fail to fully consider the unique needs and challenges of underserved populations. Understanding these challenges is vital for developing effective digital health strategies that foster inclusion and accessibility. Recent research has indicated that socio-economic barriers, cultural competency, and digital divides significantly impact the efficacy and adoption of digital health tools among these communities.

title: Predictive computational models in anesthesia and coma
summary: The transition between wakefulness and states of reduced consciousness, whether pharmacologically induced via anesthesia or pathologically necessitated by coma, remains one of the most profound challenges in modern neuroscience. While anesthesia is a controlled, reversible process, and coma is often an unpredictable, fluctuating state, both share underlying neurobiological signatures involving the disruption of global integration and local processing. Traditional clinical monitoring often relies on descriptive scales or simplified indices that may fail to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of the brain. Computational neuroscience offers a powerful framework to bridge this gap, using mathematical modeling and advanced signal processing to decode the mechanisms of unconsciousness. title: Psychological Determinants and Integrated Performance Factors in Elite Soccer
summary: Elite soccer performance has traditionally been examined through physical, technical, and tactical metrics. However, growing evidence highlights that performance in high-level competition emerges from complex interactions between cognitive processes, emotional regulation, motivational dynamics, and match context. Decision-making under pressure, attentional control, resilience, team cohesion, and psychophysiological regulation are not peripheral factors but central determinants of competitive success. At the same time, advances in soccer analytics and artificial intelligence have expanded the capacity to quantify match behavior and physiological responses. Despite these developments, psychological determinants are often examined in isolation, while data-driven performance models rarely integrate psychological constructs in a systematic and ecologically valid manner.

While MRI remains the primary modality for surveillance, imaging with radiolabeled molecules has increasingly supported the accurate diagnosis of recurrent brain lesions and treatment-related changes. title: Stem cells as immunological modulators in neurological and neurodegenerative conditions
summary: Stem cells elicit immunomodulatory properties through surface protein expression and their secretome. These properties allow stem cells to influence the immune response, reduce neuroinflammation, and create a favorable environment for neuronal survival and repair. Many neurological and neurodegenerative conditions involve chronic or dysregulated neuroinflammation, which contributes to neuronal damage. In these diseases, activated microglia and astrocytes release pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-1β), oxidative species, and other factors that exacerbate neurodegeneration. Stem cells have emerged as promising therapeutic tools due to their dual ability to promote neural regeneration and exert potent immunomodulatory effects. By restoring immune balance and supporting tissue repair, stem cells offer a multifaceted approach to treating neurodegenerative diseases with immunological components.

The synergy between these domains has enabled robots to shift from simple, repetitive executors to collaborative partners capable of handling complex tasks. Recent breakthroughs in computer vision, deep neural architectures, and sensor fusion have greatly contributed to the expanding role of smart robots across manufacturing, logistics, and inspection. title: The lymphatic system in neurodegeneration, cancer, immunity, and metabolic disease: A unifying framework for disease pathogenesis and therapy
summary: The lymphatic system is a fundamental regulator of tissue fluid balance, immune surveillance, antigen trafficking, lipid transport, macromolecular clearance, and inflammatory resolution across organ systems. Increasing evidence demonstrates that lymphatic dysfunction contributes directly to disease initiation and progression in a wide range of pathological states, including neurodegeneration, autoimmune disorders, chronic inflammatory diseases, metabolic syndromes, and cancer-related lymphedema. Across these conditions, impaired lymphatic transport may promote toxic protein accumulation, immune dysregulation, fibrosis, adipose remodeling, chronic inflammation, and failure of tissue repair.

title: Multimodal neuroimaging and clinical management of neurovascular disorders: integrating advanced MRI, CT, and intraoperative techniques
summary: Neurovascular disorders represent a significant clinical challenge within neurological and neurosurgical practice. Precise diagnosis and effective management critically depend on accurate visualization of the vasculature and brain tissue. Recent advancements in neuroimaging—particularly the refinement of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and intraoperative imaging techniques—have significantly enhanced the ability to detect, characterize, and treat these disorders with greater precision. Key questions persist regarding the optimal integration and interpretation of multimodal imaging data to inform treatment decisions, bridge the gap between anatomical and functional assessment, and improve patient outcomes. Recent studies have demonstrated that combined imaging modalities can yield complementary insights, reduce the risk of misdiagnosis, and identify nuanced pathological features that may affect clinical practice.

title: Neuromodulatory and molecular control of plastic behaviors in simple neural systems
summary: Understanding how brains adapt to changing internal states and external environments remains a central challenge in neuroscience. Simple model systems, such as Aplysia, C. elegans, and Drosophila , have long provided powerful experimental leverage to dissect how neural circuits are modified to support behavioral plasticity. These systems offer unparalleled access to the molecular, cellular, and circuit-level mechanisms through which experience and context shape action. Critically, neuromodulatory signals, ranging from monoamines to neuropeptides, play a pivotal role in dynamically reconfiguring synaptic and network states. These modulators act through diverse molecular cascades to influence protein expression, ion channel function, synaptic release machinery, and structural plasticity. Understanding these interactions will provide a tractable window into the molecular and cellular logic of behavioral adaptation.

Disruptions in these systems have been increasingly recognized as pathogenic drivers in metabolic disorders, neurocognitive dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and psychiatric conditions such as bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Recent advances in neuroimaging, digital health phenotyping, multi-omics profiling, and computational neuroscience have enabled more precise delineation of the bidirectional links between sleep physiology, energy balance, and neurobehavioral outcomes. Simultaneously, establishing animal models of human disease, large-scale epidemiological cohorts, and clinical trials has provided translational and critical insight into how environmental, nutritional, and pharmacological factors interact with sleep to shape health trajectories. summary: Environmental and occupational exposure to chemical toxicants—including pesticides, heavy metals, industrial pollutants, and food contaminants—poses a significant and growing threat to human and animal health worldwide. Despite advances in risk assessment and regulatory frameworks, the molecular mechanisms underpinning toxicant-induced organ damage remain incompletely understood, and effective therapeutic strategies are limited. Animal models continue to serve as indispensable tools for elucidating the pathophysiology of toxic organ injury and for evaluating candidate protective agents before clinical translation. By uniting toxicologists, pharmacologists, pathologists, and biomedical researchers around a shared platform, this Research Topic seeks to accelerate the translation of preclinical findings into actionable insights for public health protection.

summary: Over the past decades, cognitive science and neuroscience have experienced a conceptual shift from brain-centered models of cognition toward approaches that emphasize the dynamic relationships between brain, body, and environment. Post-cognitivist frameworks such as 4E cognition—embodied, enacted, embedded, and extended—and the related 3E cognition perspective—embodied, enacted, and environmentally scaffolded—propose that cognition emerges from continuous interactions among neural processes, bodily activity, environmental affordances, and sociocultural practices. These approaches challenge traditional views that locate cognition exclusively within neural computations. At the same time, the concept of neurodiversity has gained prominence in neuroscience and psychology, emphasizing the variability of cognitive profiles and ways of engaging with the world. title: Advances in Neuromodulation: Mechanisms, Technologies, and Clinical Applications
summary: Neuromodulation has emerged as a transformative approach for treating a wide range of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders. By delivering targeted electrical, magnetic, or chemical stimuli to specific neural circuits, neuromodulation techniques can reversibly alter neuronal activity and restore functional balance. Recent advances in technologies such as deep brain stimulation, spinal cord stimulation, and non-invasive brain stimulation have expanded therapeutic options for conditions including chronic pain, movement disorders, epilepsy, and depression. Meanwhile, growing insights into neuroimmune interactions and circuit-level mechanisms are refining our understanding of how neuromodulation exerts its effects. Despite these advances, challenges remain in optimizing stimulation parameters, improving patient-specific targeting, and elucidating long-term outcomes. title: Cognitive functions of the prefrontal cortex: Executive processes and beyond: Volume II
summary: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is a highly evolved brain region critical for orchestrating complex cognitive behaviors, decision-making, and goal-directed activity. Historically recognized as the seat of executive functions, such as working memory, planning, and cognitive flexibility, the PFC is increasingly understood to support a diverse array of cognitive operations, including social cognition, emotional regulation, and metacognitive awareness. Recent advances in neuroimaging, neurophysiology, and computational modeling continue to deepen our understanding of how the PFC integrates information across neural circuits, shaping both adaptive behavior and vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Neurotransmitter Systems in Neurodegeneration: Mechanisms, Circuits, and Therapeutic Modulation
summary: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized not only by progressive neuronal loss but also by early and sustained alterations in neurotransmission that critically shape disease onset, progression, and symptomatology. Converging evidence indicates that distinct yet partially overlapping patterns of dysfunction across dopaminergic, cholinergic, glutamatergic, GABAergic, and serotonergic systems are observed in major disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Ongoing pressures from land-use change, agricultural intensification, habitat loss, and environmental variability are reshaping plant–pollinator interactions across both natural and managed ecosystems. At the same time, increasing global demand for food underscores the importance of understanding how pollination processes contribute to resilient and sustainable food systems. Research on pollination spans diverse approaches, including field-based observations, experimental studies, and agricultural assessments. While physical inactivity, loss of muscle strength, and reduced cardiovascular fitness are known physiological contributors, psychological aspects such as negative self-perceptions of aging and exposure to ageist stereotypes also play a crucial role in shaping emotional experiences. title: AI and Machine Learning for Cognitive Decline: From Benchmarks to Clinical Practice
summary: The application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disorders has grown rapidly, with studies routinely reporting impressive accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity metrics. However, a critical gap exists between high-performing models on benchmark datasets and tools that are genuinely translatable to clinical practice. This Research Topic challenges the current paradigm of evaluating AI systems primarily through aggregate final metrics and calls for a fundamental shift toward understanding and reporting learning dynamics, that is, the processes by which models acquire, represent, and generalize knowledge in clinically relevant aging, cognitive decline, and dementia contexts. In particular, this Research Topic is interested in AI and machine learning studies that advance the understanding, assessment, prognosis, or clinical management of aging-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease.

Cognitive-emotional processes such as rumination, depressive symptoms, and negative self-evaluation serve as potential transdiagnostic risk pathways, yet their gender-specific variations and cultural expressions require further elaboration. title: Adaptive immune involvement in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and related dementias
summary: The intersection of neuroimmunology and neurodegeneration has advanced considerably in recent years, with particular interest focused on the role of the adaptive immune system in disorders such as Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and related dementias. Significant studies have revealed correlations between adaptive immune cell infiltration, neuroinflammation, and disease pathology in both human samples and animal models. For example, T cell reactivity against alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta has been observed in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's patients, respectively, while emerging data suggest that autoimmune reactions may exacerbate or modulate disease trajectories. This evolving landscape indicates a pressing need for deeper mechanistic understanding, as well as clarification of the specific immune signatures and pathways involved in diverse patient populations.

A deeper understanding of the interactions between hydrological processes and ecosystems across timescales from the palaeoenvironment to the present is therefore critically important. Such knowledge is essential for revealing the eco-hydrological impacts of climate change and for building a strong foundation to predict future trends and develop adaptive strategies that promote sustainable development and resilience in vulnerable regions.

By analyzing high-resolution environmental proxies, such as topographic variables derived from digital elevation models, the study aims to identify optimal grain sizes that enhance the detection of candidate genes under selection pressures. The research is poised to provide insights into applying multiscale variables in GEA models, advancing our understanding of species' local adaptations amidst environmental heterogeneity. Additionally, this topic will delve into the practical implications for conservation management, offering a pathway to more accurately predict and manage the genetic diversity of natural populations. The multifaceted roles of noncoding RNAs in neuroinflammatory responses
summary: Neuroinflammation is a critical process implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of a wide spectrum of central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, autoimmune conditions, and acute injury. Recent advancements have highlighted the pivotal regulatory functions of noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs)—encompassing microRNAs, long noncoding RNAs, and circular RNAs—in orchestrating inflammatory responses within the CNS. These ncRNAs modulate key signaling pathways such as NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and NLRP3, influencing transcriptional activity, mRNA stability, and cellular communication between neuronal and glial populations. While growing evidence underscores their involvement in both the amplification and resolution of inflammation, significant questions remain about the context-specific actions, regulatory networks, and interplay among distinct ncRNA species.

summary: Stroke remains one of the leading causes of long-term disability worldwide and is frequently associated with persistent motor, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral deficits. This variability underscores the urgent need for improved prognostic tools and personalized therapeutic approaches. Recent advances in neuroimaging, neurophysiology, biomechanics, and neuropsychological assessment have created new opportunities to identify biomarkers that better characterize neural plasticity and functional recovery processes. title: Therapeutic interventions and lifestyle modifications in the aging population with multiple sclerosis
summary: Advances in disease-modifying therapies, diagnostics, and comorbidity management have increased life expectancy in people with multiple sclerosis (MS), creating a growing cohort of older adults living with MS. In later life, MS typically features fewer relapses and more progressive disability, as age-related neurodegeneration, immunosenescence, polypharmacy, and accumulated disability interact with MS-specific inflammatory and neurodegenerative mechanisms. These processes, together with common comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, and arthritis, complicate symptom interpretation and make it difficult to distinguish MS progression from normal aging. Older adults frequently experience mobility limitations, cognitive decline, fatigue, mood disturbances, and urological problems, which impair quality of life and independence. Disease-modifying therapies may become less effective and carry higher risks after 55 to 60 years of age, necessitating careful reasses

title: Understanding avian intelligence: Electrophysiology of behavior and cognition
summary: Avian species have become important model organisms in behavioral neuroscience due to their capacity for complex cognitive functions supported by specialized neural architectures. Avian species exhibit a broad behavioral repertoire, including intricate problem-solving abilities, communication abilities via vocal learning, dynamic social behavior, and tool use. These features provide a powerful comparative framework for examining the evolutionary trajectories of intelligence and the implementation of cognitive functions across vertebrate brains.
image_alt: Understanding avian intelligence: Electrophysiology of behavior and cognition

summary: This Collection seeks to highlight cutting-edge research on electrical and thermal transport mechanisms in materials designed for energy conversion and storage, with a particular focus on solid-state batteries, perovskite solar cells, 2D materials, fuel cells and organic semiconductors.

title: Emotional state transitions: cellular, molecular and circuit mechanisms of safety, fear, aggression, and trauma
summary: Emotional states in animals are thought to be encoded by the coordinated activity of distributed brain networks, triggered by specific external stimuli. Although the precise definition of emotions remains debated, there is broad agreement that emotional states manifest as overtly observable behaviors, often accompanied by physiological responses. A central unresolved question is whether emotional states are drivers or consequences of behavioral responses, and how neural circuit activity generates, stabilizes and allows transitions between positive (safety and appetitive) and negative (fear, aggression, and trauma) valence states.
image_alt: Emotional state transitions: cellular, molecular and circuit mechanisms of safety, fear, aggression, and trauma

title: Imaging-Guided Neuromodulation for Brain Cognitive Function Enhancement: Methodological Advances in Targeting, Biomarkers, and Validation
summary: Neuroimaging has become central to cognitive enhancement research, transforming non-invasive neuromodulation from an empirical practice into a mechanistically grounded discipline. Today, neuroregulatory technologies — including transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), TMS, neurofeedback, and emerging modalities such as tFUS and TIS — are routinely paired with fMRI, fNIRS, and EEG. This coupling shifts cognitive enhancement from behavioral observation toward mechanistic exploration: imaging defines cortical targets, monitors interventions in real time, and validates stimulation effects at the network level. Yet critical methodological gaps remain. Artifact contamination in simultaneous stimulation–imaging recordings, multi-site inconsistencies, limited reliability of imaging biomarkers, and weak causal links between stimulation, imaging changes, and cognitive outcomes all constrain reproducibility and individualization.

title: Innovative interventions in neurorehabilitation: New techniques and discoveries
summary: Neurorehabilitation is a critical field addressing recovery and functional restoration in individuals with neurological injuries and disorders, including stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's disease, and other neurodegenerative conditions. Traditional rehabilitation approaches have shown promising results, but the evolving landscape of neuroscience research has opened new avenues for innovation. Advanced neuroimaging, brain-computer interfaces, pharmacological interventions, and novel therapeutic techniques are reshaping how we approach patient recovery. Understanding and implementing these cutting-edge interventions is essential for improving outcomes, enhancing quality of life, and optimizing recovery trajectories across diverse patient populations.

title: Neurological Biomarkers for Drug Delivery Systems in Blood–Brain Barrier Research
summary: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective, semipermeable border of endothelial cells that protects the brain from potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream while allowing the passage of essential nutrients. While this protective function is vital for maintaining central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis, it also presents a formidable challenge for the delivery of therapeutic agents to treat neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson’s, brain tumors, epilepsy, and multiple sclerosis.
image_alt: Neurological Biomarkers for Drug Delivery Systems in Blood–Brain Barrier Research

title: Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Control and Optimization: Overcoming Real-World Deployment Bottlenecks
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable potential for acquiring complex robotic skills, from agile locomotion to in-hand manipulation. Yet the transition of these policies from simulation to physical systems remains deeply unreliable. The field faces a set of urgent, unsolved bottlenecks: extreme sample inefficiency makes training on hardware prohibitively expensive; the lack of rigorous safety guarantees prevents deployment in human-shared environments; policies brittlely fail under visual and dynamical distribution shifts; and sim-to-real transfer continues to demand laborious manual tuning. While traditional control theory provides stability and structure, it cannot alone address these data-driven adaptation and generalization challenges—and current RL methods have not yet closed this gap. There is now a pressing need for RL algorithms that are not only performant but also sample-efficient, safe, transferable, and amenable to real-time hardware constraints. This Rese
