title: Health Monitoring for Management, Welfare, and Conservation of Animals In Situ and Ex Situ
summary: Health monitoring plays a fundamental role in understanding and managing animal populations, whether in natural ecosystems or controlled environments. In recent decades, growing environmental pressures and increased awareness of animal welfare have highlighted the need for robust and integrative health assessment approaches. Traditional methods, often invasive or limited in scope, are being complemented by emerging tools such as non-invasive sampling, remote sensing, and behavioural indicators. Despite these advances, challenges persist in standardising methodologies, integrating multidisciplinary data, and applying findings across in situ and ex situ contexts. Addressing these gaps is essential to improving conservation outcomes, optimising management strategies, and ensuring high welfare standards across diverse species and settings.

title: Innovative applications of fNIRS in brain and behavioral studies
summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a unique combination of temporal resolution, ecological validity, and practical flexibility that complements and, in many contexts, surpasses the constraints of traditional neuroimaging approaches. fNIRS enables continuous, non-invasive monitoring of cortical hemodynamics with minimal susceptibility to motion artifacts — a critical advantage when studying populations and behaviors that are incompatible with conventional laboratory settings.

title: Targeting Neuroinflammation: Mechanisms, Pathways and Therapeutic Opportunities
summary: Neuroinflammation is a critical pathological process at the intersection of immunology and neuroscience. It is now established as a key driver in the onset and progression of a wide range of central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, and depression. The complex interplay between activated glial cells, inflammatory signaling, and neuronal function presents both a significant challenge and a compelling opportunity for therapeutic intervention. Despite significant advances in understanding these mechanisms, effective pharmacological treatments targeting neuroinflammation remain scarce outside of broad immunosuppressive approaches.

title: Tumor Microenvironment Complexity and its Therapeutic Implications - Volume II
summary: The tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a cornerstone in understanding cancer biology, functioning as a dynamic ecosystem composed of cancer cells, fibroblasts, immune cells, extracellular matrix components, pericytes, and blood vessels. Since the publication of the first volume of this Research Topic, new insights have reinforced the critical role of the TME in shaping tumor aggressiveness, metastatic behavior, and therapeutic resistance. In Veterinary Oncology, the integration of TME research has continued to evolve, though it still lags human biomedical research. The comparative investigation of naturally occurring cancers in companion animals provides a translational opportunity to unveil mechanisms of tumor progression relevant to both human and veterinary patients. Despite significant progress, the comprehensive understanding of TME architecture and function in companion animals remains in its infancy. Recent studies have revealed how specific TME components—such as immune cell

title: Veterinary Forensic Pathology: New Directions in Post-Mortem Interval and Animal Remains Identification
summary: Veterinary thanatology and clinicopathology together form a vital and evolving interface within veterinary science, linking the processes of life and death. This integrated perspective deepens understanding of how ante mortem clinical conditions influence post mortem changes, contributing meaningfully to diagnostic precision, forensic reliability, and species specific knowledge. Although accurate post mortem interval (PMI) estimation and identification of animal remains underpin critical applications in veterinary forensics, wildlife conservation, agricultural incidents, and disaster response, the field has largely relied on adaptations from human forensic methodologies. Such dependencies have led to inconsistencies in accuracy across animal taxa, given the diversity in physiology, metabolism, and environmental exposure. Recent findings point to considerable discrepancies in the decomposition timeline and post mortem tissue markers across species. Alongside these challenges, growing ev

title: Critical perspectives on gendered mental health issues/women’s mental health
summary: Objectives: • To publish examples of excellent interdisciplinary work on women’s mental health • To encourage conceptual frameworks for approaching women’s mental health as an interdisciplinary and intersectional problem • To contribute to new ways of tackling the gendered mental illness gap as a longstanding and life long health problem • To highlight reproductive transitional periods that are unique to women, including the perinatal period and perimenopause, as important contexts for interdisciplinary mental health research

title: From 5G to Satellite: AI Approaches for Energy-Efficient, High-Performance Network Infrastructures
summary: The exponential growth in data traffic, driven by 5G/6G rollout, cloud computing, real-time applications, and massive IoT deployment, places increasing strain on high-speed network infrastructures. Conventional, rule-based network management cannot adapt quickly enough to dynamic traffic patterns, resulting in inefficient energy use and degraded performance. Artificial intelligence, including deep reinforcement learning, federated learning, graph neural networks, and large language models, offers a path toward networks that self-optimize, predict demand, and conserve energy without sacrificing throughput or latency.
image_alt: From 5G to Satellite: AI Approaches for Energy-Efficient, High-Performance Network Infrastructures

title: Human-Wildlife Interactions in Urban Environments: Conflicts, Drivers, and Pathways for Coexistence
summary: The continuous intensification of human–wildlife interactions in cities is an emerging global challenge that reflects broader environmental transitions, including urbanisation, climate change, land-use change, and habitat fragmentation, as well as social transformations such as shifting public and governmental attitudes toward nature. As wildlife species adapt to urban landscapes, their interactions with people become more frequent and more complex, spanning a wide spectrum from conflict and risk to tolerance, coexistence, and mutual adaptation. Recent research has shown that the nature and intensity of these interactions are shaped not only by ecological factors but also by human perceptions, cultural norms, gender, educational level, and socio-economic conditions. Long-term monitoring, cross-cultural and geographic comparisons, and social-ecological approaches have revealed substantial temporal changes in both wildlife behaviour and public expectations. title: Multi-objective Forest Management under Global Change: Forest Ecosystem Response Mechanisms and Resource Utilization
summary: Against the backdrop of global change—characterized by climate warming, shifting precipitation patterns, and intensified anthropogenic disturbances—the ecological and economic values of forest ecosystems are facing increasingly complex challenges. Forests worldwide encompass a broad continuum, ranging from natural, undisturbed, and minimally managed forests to intensively managed plantations and production forests. Understanding forest ecosystem responses to global change is essential for biodiversity conservation, ecosystem service maintenance, climate adaptation, and sustainable resource use. This Research Topic focuses on forest ecosystem service functions within the context of global change, with an emphasis on analyzing response and adaptation mechanisms, as well as exploring multi-objective utilization strategies for forest resources.

title: Robotics at a Crossroads: AI-Based vs Classical Methods in Control, HRI, and Autonomy
summary: The field of robotics is undergoing a profound transformation driven by rapid advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models and vision-language models. These AI-based approaches are increasingly being integrated into robotic systems for control, decision-making, perception, and human-robot interaction, often demonstrating remarkable capabilities in generalisation and adaptability. At the same time, classical methods—rooted in well-established control theory, model-based planning, and rule-based systems—continue to offer reliability, interpretability, and formal guarantees that remain essential in safety-critical applications. This evolving landscape raises fundamental questions about when and how AI-driven approaches should complement or replace traditional techniques, and whether hybrid models combining classical and AI-based methods can leverage the strengths of both paradigms. title: Hosts, Parasites, and Pathogens in a Warming World
summary: Global warming is transforming the ecological and evolutionary balance of host–parasite–pathogen systems. Rising temperatures affect the development of parasites and vectors, expand geographic ranges of vectors, and alter host immune responses, leading to the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases across humans, livestock, and wildlife. At the same time, parasitic infections can disrupt host microbiota which may exacerbate heat stress mediated microbial dysbiosis, increasing the susceptibility of hosts to opportunistic pathogens. Greater climate variability is also driving the evolution of parasites and pathogens that can withstand extreme conditions, intensifying disease transmission and drug resistance. Soil ecosystems are equally affected; climate change influences nematode and microbial communities with long-term consequences for soil health, biodiversity, and food security. title: MRI techniques for assessing brain mechanics and injury
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays a pivotal role in advancing our understanding of brain mechanics and the pathological processes underlying traumatic and degenerative injuries. In recent years, progress in MRI-based techniques, such as magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), diffusion MRI (dMRI), and functional MRI (fMRI), has expanded our capacity to quantify brain tissue stiffness, microstructural organization, and functional connectivity. Despite these developments, the biophysical interpretation of imaging markers, their sensitivity to early mechanical abnormalities, and the translation of these measurements from research to clinical practice remain limited. Current debates in the field center on how to standardize MRI-based mechanical metrics, link them to histopathological changes, and integrate multimodal data to identify early signatures of injury progression. title: Beyond the single neuron: computational principles of distributed neural coding in the age of large-scale recordings
summary: Neural coding is the fundamental language of the brain, the set of rules by which stimulus features and internal states are transformed into electrical signals. Historically, research focused on the properties of single neurons, emphasizing firing rates and receptive field tuning. However, a major paradigm shift is underway, moving toward the study of distributed representations where information is encoded in the collective activity of large-scale neural ensembles. From the precision of spike-timing, to the robustness of population vectors and high-dimensional manifolds, the principles governing neural representation are remarkably diverse. The central problem this Research Topic addresses is the absence of a unified theoretical framework bridging microscopic neural activity and macroscopic functional representations. title: Multimodal Annotation for Intangible Cultural Heritage: Embodied Knowledge and Technology
summary: The field of Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) preservation increasingly depends on multimodal data, ranging from motion capture to volumetric video and sensory recordings, yet current digital documentation still reflects a largely product-oriented paradigm. This approach privileges outcomes rather than the creative, embodied, and processual dimensions of transmission. Recent research across digital humanities, performance studies, and human-computer interaction calls for a process-oriented shift that understands multimodal annotation not simply as record-keeping, but as a dynamic, interpretative practice. Landmark projects such as TKB, BlackBox, Motion Bank, and Arvest have illustrated how digital notebooks and hybrid archives can encode tacit knowledge, making performance and creative practices computationally addressable while preserving their embodied nature. title: Social Isolation, Social Participation, and Health Outcomes in Older Adults
summary: Research on ageing populations increasingly highlights the profound effects of social connectedness on health and well-being in later life. Social isolation is recognized as a significant risk factor for a range of adverse health outcomes among older adults, including cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, depression, and reduced quality of life. While social participation is frequently associated with more positive physical and psychological outcomes, the mechanisms linking these factors remain insufficiently explored. The rapid uptake of digital technology, particularly smartphones, introduces both opportunities and challenges to the social integration of older people. Despite a growing body of research, much of the current literature is fragmented and lacks a holistic view of how overlapping social, technological, and psychological variables interact to shape health trajectories among older adults.

title: Differential drug responsiveness in addiction: Multivariate determinants across psychostimulants and opioids
summary: Not all drug users are the same. To understand different profiles of patients that use addictive substances, research frameworks typically classify cases by drug class and severity of compulsive use. However, individuals exposed to the same psychostimulant or opioid under similar conditions vary markedly in motivation to obtain the drug, effort expenditure, sensitivity to punishment or constraint, relapse vulnerability, and transitions between drug classes. Psychostimulants and opioids engage overlapping but distinct neural systems within mesolimbic and cortico-striatal circuits, yet these differences are rarely examined within unified cross-drug frameworks.

summary: Movement disorders encompass a broad range of neurological conditions characterized by hypokinetic, hyperkinetic states, or both. The abnormal expression of voluntary movement can be measured in the clinical setting using a variety of tools. There is increasing evidence that these technological advancements can enhance the accuracy of diagnosis and clinical decisions on treatments. Despite considerable progress, challenges remain in achieving early diagnosis, continuous monitoring, and personalized treatment strategies.

title: GeoAI and Foundation Models for Ecological Remote Sensing and Sustainable Ecosystem Management
summary: The accelerating pace of global environmental change driven by climate change, biodiversity loss, land degradation, and urbanization demands transformative approaches to ecosystem monitoring and sustainable resource management. Recent advances in Earth observation technologies, together with rapid progress in Artificial Intelligence (AI), GeoAI, and geospatial foundation models, are revolutionising our ability to observe, understand, and manage Earth's ecosystems at unprecedented spatial and temporal scales.

title: Innovative signal processing algorithms: Machine learning, deep learning, AI
summary: The human brain generates an extraordinary volume of complex, high-dimensional signals, from electroencephalographic (EEG) and magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings to functional MRI time series and intracranial local field potentials. Decoding these signals with sufficient precision to advance our understanding of neural function and to translate that understanding into clinical tools, represents one of the defining challenges of modern neuroscience. Conventional signal processing approaches, while foundational, are increasingly insufficient in the face of data complexity, inter-subject variability, and the subtlety of neural dynamics that underlie cognition, perception, and disease.

title: Oncoethics in Transition: Ethical Challenges and Policy Responses Across the Cancer Care Continuum
summary: Ethical challenges are inherent to healthcare and are particularly pronounced in oncology and cancer-related palliative care. Patients and their families often face profound vulnerability following diagnosis, during complex treatment trajectories, in transition, and at the end of life. These situations involve high levels of uncertainty, emotional distress, and a high probability of competing values. Ethical tensions may arise at the (inter-)personal, (inter-)professional, and systemic levels—for example, between autonomy and beneficence, innovation and equity, or prolongation of life and quality of life. At the same time, rapid developments in cancer therapies, increasing use of digital technologies, and persistent inequities in access to care further intensify these challenges. How health systems and public policy respond to these tensions—through governance structures, regulatory frameworks, resource allocation decisions, and standards of care—shapes ethical outcomes at both individ

title: Sex Differences in Adult Glioblastoma and Paediatric-type High-Grade Gliomas: Biology, Therapeutic Response, and Resistance Mechanisms
summary: High-grade gliomas remain among the most aggressive primary brain tumors. In adults, glioblastoma (GBM, IDH-wildtype) dominates, whereas paediatric-type diffuse high-grade gliomas — including diffuse midline glioma (H3 K27-altered) and diffuse hemispheric glioma (H3 G34-mutant) — represent distinct, molecularly defined entities. Across both groups, tumors exhibit marked heterogeneity in disease progression, treatment response, and patient outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests that biological sex significantly influences their incidence, tumor microenvironment, immune regulation, metabolic reprogramming, therapeutic efficacy, and mechanisms of resistance. However, sex-specific molecular pathways and their translational implications remain insufficiently understood.

title: Shape, Stress, and Disease: Morphological Biomarkers Across Taxa and Ecosystems in a Changing World.
summary: Environmental stressors, including climate change, habitat fragmentation, pollution, agricultural intensification, and urbanization, are changing the physical forms of organisms across all major groups of life. These morphological changes can act as early-warning signals for disease outbreaks, crop failure, and ecosystem breakdown.

title: The Parkinsonian Spectrum: Dissecting Convergent Mechanisms
summary: The etiology of the progressive neurodegeneration that characterizes Parkinson’s disease (PD) remains relatively enigmatic, despite immense advances in our understanding of the condition. Pivotal elements that underpin current viewpoints include vital contributions from both molecular genetics and also from greatly improved understanding of the nature of aggregated proteins, which carry the potential to propagate throughout the nervous system.
image_alt: The Parkinsonian Spectrum: Dissecting Convergent Mechanisms

title: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics in Human-Dominated Systems: Data-Driven Insights for Conservation and Sustainability
summary: Human activity now shapes the majority of the planet’s ecosystems. Urbanisation, land-use change, agriculture, and environmental disturbance are altering habitats, reshaping species distributions, and driving rapid ecological and evolutionary responses in the organisms and communities that persist within human-dominated landscapes. At the same time, the digitalisation of environmental observation has produced unprecedented volumes of data, from remote sensing and biodiversity monitoring to sensor networks and citizen science, opening new opportunities to study these dynamics at scales and resolutions that were previously impossible.

title: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics of Wildlife and Marine Holobionts under Environmental Change
summary: The holobiont concept — the recognition of animals and their associated microbial communities as integrated functional and evolutionary units — has reshaped how biologists understand symbiosis, adaptation, and resilience in wild populations. Across wildlife and marine systems, host-microbe partnerships are increasingly viewed as the product of long evolutionary histories of reciprocal selection, co-adaptation, and phylosymbiosis, in which microbial communities both shape and are shaped by host biology. Yet much of the holobiont literature remains descriptive, with limited mechanistic insight into how these partnerships are assembled, transmitted, and reshaped by the ecological and evolutionary pressures that wild animals face.

title: Enabling Sustainable Return-to-Work and Reintegration After Illness and Chronic Conditions
summary: Population aging represents one of the major challenges for occupational and healthcare systems in industrialized countries. The increase in retirement age, together with demographic changes and the progressive extension of working life, has led to a growing proportion of older workers within the labor market. At the same time, the rising average age of the workforce is associated with a higher prevalence of chronic diseases, multimorbidity, and health conditions that may result in prolonged sickness absence.

title: Energy absorption mechanisms in structural systems
summary: This Collection brings together research exploring energy absorption mechanisms in structural systems, highlighting experimental and technological developments that drive solutions in modern structural systems.

title: Explorations of alternative constructs to presence in Augmented and Mixed reality
summary: The concept of "presence" in VR is often defined as "the sense of being there," where "there" often refers to a virtual environment. While it is very broadly accepted that presence is a foundational phenomenon in immersive experiences, there is some debate in the community as to what presence actually is defined as and what is the best way to measure it. Given the different standpoints on definitions, researchers have built different, primarily subjective, measures, which do share some similarities but differ in scope. There is further discussion on the nature of presence in AR and MR experiences where there is a lack of the place illusion (PI), which is a key component in measuring presence. Debates tend to center on whether presence can be measured in AR/MR, how it should be measured in AR/MR, and what "there" is if there's no virtual environment.

Neural basis of substance use and addiction: Recent findings and treatment implications
summary: Addiction remains one of the most pressing public health challenges of our time, and the landscape is shifting fast. The rise of synthetic opioids and polysubstance use, the explosion of behavioral and digital addictions (gaming, social media, gambling), and breakthrough treatments once considered fringe — such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and psychedelic-assisted therapies — have transformed both the questions we ask and the tools we use to answer them. At the same time, advances in human neuroscience, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence are giving us unprecedented resolution into the neural mechanisms that drive compulsive behavior and, crucially, recovery.

title: Next-gen neuro-AI: Aligning foundation models and biologically plausible architectures with human cognition
summary: Cognitive computational neuroscience has entered a transformative era. The rapid rise of large multimodal foundation models, state-space architectures, and advanced transformers has shifted the conversation: we are no longer just building artificial intelligence to solve tasks, but actively using these models as candidate mathematical "theories of the mind." By comparing the latent representations of artificial neural networks with biological neural activity, researchers are uncovering unprecedented insights into human perception, memory, decision-making, and language.

title: Sleep to Think: Multimodal Mechanisms Linking Sleep, Learning, and Performance
summary: Sleep is not merely a passive state but a dynamic process fundamental to learning, memory consolidation, and cognitive performance. During sleep, the brain undergoes remarkable transformations—reorganizing neural circuits, strengthening newly acquired memories, and clearing metabolic waste accumulated during wakefulness. Decades of research have established that adequate sleep enhances learning capacity, improves problem-solving, and optimizes performance across academic, athletic, and professional domains. Conversely, sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory, and executive function. Yet the precise multimodal mechanisms linking sleep architecture, electrophysiological activity, neurochemical processes, and behavioral outcomes remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in polysomnography, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, computational modeling, and biomarker assessment have enabled more sophisticated investigation of sleep-dependent learning and performance. summary: This Collection calls for papers that investigate the expanding clinical and biological roles of GLP‑1 RAs. title: Nutrition and mood disorders: Mechanistic insights, preclinical models, and clinical perspectives
summary: Mood disorders, including depression and anxiety, are rising at an alarming rate and represent one of today’s most pressing global health challenges. Their etiology is multifactorial, involving complex interactions between genetic, environmental, lifestyle, and neurobiological factors. Central to these disorders are alterations in brain plasticity, disruptions in cognitive processing, and persistent low-grade neuroinflammation, each of which contributes to the onset and progression of mood symptoms. Dysregulation in synaptic remodeling, impairments in executive function and memory, and heightened pro-inflammatory signaling (e.g., via microglia and cytokine cascades) are now widely recognized as central to these disorders.
image_alt: Nutrition and mood disorders: Mechanistic insights, preclinical models, and clinical perspectives

title: Reimagining Human Movement: The Impact of Extended Reality on Physical and Emotional Experience, Volume II
summary: Extended Reality (XR), encompassing Virtual, Augmented, and Mixed Reality, has rapidly moved from novelty to a credible tool for shaping how humans learn, train, recover, and express movement. Volume I of this Research Topic attracted broad engagement across motor learning, neurorehabilitation, sport performance, and creative movement, confirming a vibrant interdisciplinary community working at the intersection of immersive technology and human physicality. It also exposed three areas where the evidence base remains thin: durable, long-term effects of XR-based movement training; applications across the full lifespan, in particular healthy aging and clinical populations; and inclusive, equitable design of immersive movement experiences. Volume II builds directly on this momentum, deepening the scientific conversation rather than restarting it, and broadening the contributor pool toward clinical, developmental, and applied settings.
image_alt: Reimagining Human Movement: The Impact of Extended Reality on Physical and Emotional Experience, Volume II

title: Review the Potential of Imaging Biomarkers in the Diagnosis and Prognosis of Neuro-Oncology
summary: Neuroimaging plays several fundamental roles in the management of animals with tumors of the nervous system, including diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response assessment. Despite the demonstrated clinical utility and advantages of neuroimaging, numerous challenges remain that underscore the continuing need for neuroimaging methods that can improve diagnostic accuracy and non-invasively interrogate clinically relevant phenotypic and pathophysiologic aspects of nervous system neoplasms before and after treatment. The objective of this research topic is to highlight recent research that improves the capabilities of, expands applications for, or overcomes previously identified challenges of neuroimaging modalities and techniques for the diagnosis, treatment, or prognostication of animals with tumors affecting the nervous system. By contributing to the collective knowledge in the field, this research topic hopes to foster an informed approach to provision of neuro-oncological care, a

title: AI-Enabled Trial Matching and Adaptive Trials in Pediatric Oncology
summary: Pediatric oncology represents a crucial and rapidly evolving field within precision medicine, distinguished by the rarity and diversity of childhood cancers as well as their intricate molecular underpinnings. Although notable progress has been made in diagnostic techniques and therapeutic interventions, children lag behind adults in clinical trial enrollment, constraining the pace of innovation and the equitable application of novel therapies. This limited representation stems from the challenges inherent to conducting trials within small, heterogeneous patient populations and the logistical and ethical hurdles of pediatric research. In response, artificial intelligence (AI) has begun to reshape the landscape of trial design by facilitating personalized prognosis, optimizing cohort selection, and enabling real-time adaptation. AI-driven systems are harnessing multi-modal data—encompassing genomics, imaging, and electronic health records—to refine eligibility criteria and treatment matc
image_alt: AI-Enabled Trial Matching and Adaptive Trials in Pediatric Oncology

title: Beyond adolescence: cannabinoid exposure during extended human brain development
summary: Over the past decade in the United States, cannabis use has risen dramatically, with daily or near-daily consumption now affecting an estimated 18 million individuals, up from approximately 6 million in 2012 and fewer than one million in 1992. In parallel, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) potency in commercial products has increased substantially, with many legal-market preparations now exceeding 20%, far above historical levels. While legalization has expanded access, regulatory frameworks have not consistently kept pace, raising concerns about public health and neurodevelopmental risk. The endocannabinoid system is a key regulator of brain maturation, governing synaptic pruning, circuit refinement, and excitatory–inhibitory balance via CB1 receptors densely expressed in corticolimbic regions. Δ9-THC exposure during sensitive developmental windows may disrupt these processes, altering prefrontal circuit maturation and producing lasting impairments in cognitive control and executive funct
image_alt: Beyond adolescence: cannabinoid exposure during extended human brain development

title: Brain–body interactions in neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders
summary: Understanding the complex communication between the brain and peripheral systems has become central to human neuroscience. Recent research highlights that the central nervous system interacts dynamically with the immune, endocrine, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems, influencing both brain function and behaviour across the lifespan. Dysregulation in these bidirectional networks is increasingly implicated in the development and progression of neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, schizophrenia, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. Emerging evidence from neuroimaging, multi-omics, and clinical studies underscores the role of systemic inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and gut–brain signalling in shaping cognitive and emotional processes. Despite these advances, a comprehensive understanding of how brain–body interactions contribute to the onset, progression, and treatment response of these disorders remains incomplete. Addressing this gap re
image_alt: Brain–body interactions in neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders

title: Decision Architectures in Ethology: Linking Molecules, Brains, Behavior, and Ecology
summary: A unifying challenge in ethology is to understand how animals construct and use internal decision rules to navigate complex, changing environments. Across taxa, behavior emerges from interactions among molecular signals, neural circuits, development, and ecological and social context, yet these elements are often studied in isolation. Bringing them together under the lens of “decision architectures” offers a way to compare species, levels of organization, and timescales, and to discover general principles of how choices are structured, constrained, and modified by experience and evolution. Situating ethological research in this framework opens space for contributions that are mechanistic, theoretical, and comparative, while remaining grounded in real organisms behaving in naturalistic or ecologically relevant settings.
image_alt: Decision Architectures in Ethology: Linking Molecules, Brains, Behavior, and Ecology

title: Multimodal data integration for precision brain health
summary: Breakthroughs in human neuroscience have enabled the generation of diverse and high-dimensional data from genomics and epigenomics, advanced neuroimaging, fluid and digital biomarkers, as well as cognitive and behavioral assessments. Despite these advances, single-modality studies often fall short in capturing the complexity of brain health and disease, leaving gaps in our understanding of nervous system development, mechanisms underlying neuropsychiatric and neurological conditions, and factors affecting brain aging. Recent research has demonstrated the potential of integrating data across multiple biological and behavioral domains to uncover novel biomarkers, patient subtypes, and mechanistic insights. However, challenges remain around analytic integration, clinical translation, and ensuring reproducibility and equity in findings.
image_alt: Multimodal data integration for precision brain health

title: Neonatal Brain Injury and Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcomes: From Early Prediction to Lifelong Care
summary: Neonatal brain injury remains a major cause of mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment worldwide. Conditions such as hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, prematurity-related brain injury, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, neonatal stroke, and central nervous system infections can have lasting effects on cognitive, motor, behavioral, and functional development. As advances in neonatal intensive care continue to improve survival rates, increasing attention has shifted toward understanding and optimizing long-term outcomes for affected infants.
image_alt: Neonatal Brain Injury and Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcomes: From Early Prediction to Lifelong Care

title: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury
summary: Spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to devastating and often irreversible loss of sensory and motor function due to the limited regenerative capacity of the adult central nervous system. Axon regeneration, the ability of injured neurons to re-extend functional projections, is a critical prerequisite for restoring connectivity and neurological recovery. Despite decades of research, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern axon regeneration remain only partially understood. This Research Topic aims to highlight emerging molecular and cellular targets that drive axon regeneration following spinal cord injury. By integrating discoveries from transcriptomic profiling, genetic manipulation, and advanced imaging, this collection seeks to uncover new regulatory pathways and therapeutic strategies that promote axonal growth and synaptic reconnection after injury.
image_alt: Novel Molecular and Cellular Targets Driving Axon Regeneration After Spinal Cord Injury

Pushed to Choose: Motivational, Emotional, and Physiological Processes in Police Decision-Making
summary: Police decision-making often unfolds in emotionally charged, uncertain, and time-pressured environments. Officers are required to interpret ambiguous cues, regulate affect, assess risk, and act in ways that are lawful, proportionate, and operationally effective. Yet these decisions are not shaped by cognition alone. Emotional states, chronic occupational stress, fatigue, burnout, trauma exposure, moral strain, and psychological well-being can all influence attention, judgment, impulse control, communication, and post-incident recovery. At the same time, the consequences of police decisions extend beyond individual performance to public trust, procedural justice, use-of-force outcomes, and officers’ long-term mental health. A focused discussion of how emotional processes and well-being interact with police decision-making is therefore timely and necessary, both for psychological theory and for evidence-informed practice.
image_alt: Pushed to Choose: Motivational, Emotional, and Physiological Processes in Police Decision-Making

title: Remodeling of blood-brain barrier function: implications for stroke therapy and clinical translation
summary: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), typically caused by hypertension or aneurysm rupture, is a devastating subtype of stroke. ICH accounts for approximately 15% of all stroke cases and is characterized by high mortality and morbidity. Despite advances in neurocritical care, clinical interventions such as hematoma evacuation rarely improve neurological outcomes. Studies have found that ICH causes not only primary brain injury but also secondary brain injury after hemorrhage, in which disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a central event, contributing to peri-hematomal edema, hematoma expansion, and ultimately neuronal damage. The neurovascular unit (NVU) is the core component of the BBB and is composed of endothelial cells, astrocytes, pericytes, neurons, and the extracellular matrix.

title: The Role of Mental Health Factors in the Prevention and Management of Musculoskeletal Disorders: A Psychiatric Perspective
summary: The intersection of psychiatry and musculoskeletal health has become an increasingly significant field of study, revealing how psychological, biological, and social factors interact to influence physical well-being. Recent research indicates that musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) such as chronic pain, fibromyalgia, and back disorders are not purely biomechanical conditions but are profoundly shaped by mental health factors including stress, anxiety, depression, and coping mechanisms. Studies have shown that these disorders can worsen psychological distress, while psychiatric conditions may contribute to the onset or progression of physical symptoms—creating a bidirectional relationship. Despite increasing recognition of this interplay, the mechanisms underlying these interactions remain insufficiently understood. Current models often treat physical and mental health separately, overlooking the potential benefits of integrated prevention and management strategies that address both dimens

title: Translational brain imaging–guided neuromodulation
summary: The intersection of advanced neuroimaging and neuromodulation is reshaping how we understand and treat disorders of the nervous system. Techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and focused ultrasound have matured considerably over the past two decades. Yet their clinical impact has remained constrained by a fundamental gap: stimulation protocols are rarely informed by the individual’s brain structure and function. Neuroimaging is poised to close that gap. By mapping functional connectivity, cortical excitability, white matter architecture, and network-level dynamics, we can now move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches and toward precision neuromodulation grounded in the living brain’s own organization.
image_alt: Translational brain imaging–guided neuromodulation

title: Virtual Reality for Mental Health: Behavioral Interventions, Therapy, Protocols, and Affective Regulation
summary: Recent advances in immersive technologies have positioned Virtual Reality (VR) as a powerful tool for mental health assessment and intervention. In particular, Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET) and VR-based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (VR-CBT) have demonstrated effectiveness in treating anxiety disorders, phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). These approaches enable controlled, safe, and ecologically valid environments where emotional and behavioral responses can be elicited, monitored, and modified in real time. Despite promising results, challenges remain in standardizing therapeutic protocols, understanding long-term outcomes, and integrating physiological and behavioral data into adaptive interventions. This Research Topic addresses the need for rigorous, interdisciplinary research that advances VR-based mental health interventions grounded in clinical evidence and behavioral science.
image_alt: Virtual Reality for Mental Health: Behavioral Interventions, Therapy, Protocols, and Affective Regulation

title: After-Work Recovery in Hybrid Work: Remote Work Intensity, Personal Resources, and Recovery Outcomes
summary: The boundaries between work and non-work life have never been more blurred. As hybrid arrangements consolidate as the dominant model in knowledge-intensive sectors, employees increasingly move between professional and personal domains — often within the same physical space. While hybrid work offers autonomy and flexibility, growing evidence suggests it also reshapes the psychological mechanisms through which employees disengage from work, recover from daily demands, and protect their well-being. In this context, the rapid evolution of digital tools and the pervasiveness of communication technologies have introduced new complexities, making individual coping strategies to manage digital demands and psychologically detach from work a critical area of investigation.
image_alt: After-Work Recovery in Hybrid Work: Remote Work Intensity, Personal Resources, and Recovery Outcomes

title: Human-AI Interaction for Learning: Cognitive, Linguistic and Institutional Futures in the Global South
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping education through adaptive learning systems, generative tools, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring and human-computer interaction. However, the central question is no longer only what AI can do, but how learners, educators and institutions interact with AI in ways that support cognition, inclusion, human agency and educational purpose. Work on neuro-cognitive STEM enhancement foregrounds the relationship between cognitive factors, STEM achievement, human-brain/computer interface, cognitive adaptability and personalised learning. In the South African higher education context, AI adoption also raises urgent questions about human-centredness, inequality, ethics, regulation and institutional readiness. Internationally, UNESCO similarly emphasises that generative AI in education should be guided by human agency, inclusion, equity, linguistic diversity, privacy and pedagogical appropriateness.
image_alt: Human-AI Interaction for Learning: Cognitive, Linguistic and Institutional Futures in the Global South

title: Edge AI for Robotics: Emerging Technologies and Applications
summary: Edge AI enables AI models to run directly on local devices, bringing computation closer to data sources for faster, more efficient decision-making. Therefore, it is critical for modern robotics, where rapid and robust decision-making is essential. In applications such as high-speed drones and industrial robots operating in extreme conditions, on-device processing ensures real-time control and reliability. Moreover, as service robots become increasingly integrated into daily and personal environments, preserving user privacy during data processing is paramount. While recent advances in AI and deep learning have significantly enhanced robotic capabilities in perception, decision-making, and control, relying solely on cloud-based processing can introduce delays and compromise privacy. Leveraging edge AI enables decentralized, real-time computation that meets the demanding requirements of today's robotic applications.
image_alt: Edge AI for Robotics: Emerging Technologies and Applications

title: Emotional dysregulation, compulsivity, and obsessive-like behaviors across addictions: Neurobiological, psychological, and transdiagnostic perspectives
summary: Emotional dysregulation and compulsivity are widespread but mechanistically underexplored dimensions that cut across substance use disorders, behavioral addictions, and a broader spectrum of maladaptive and addiction-like behaviors. Despite their growing clinical relevance, how these dimensions interact and reinforce one another in self-perpetuating cycles remains insufficiently characterized at both the neurobiological and psychological levels. Alongside emotional dysregulation and compulsivity, obsessive-like behaviors add a further dimension, reflecting the repetitive, intrusive, and rigid action patterns frequently observed across addictive phenotypes, reinforcing their transdiagnostic nature.
image_alt: Emotional dysregulation, compulsivity, and obsessive-like behaviors across addictions: Neurobiological, psychological, and transdiagnostic perspectives

title: Ethical Impact of Artificial Intelligence in Neurorehabilitation
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the landscape of neurorehabilitation, offering new avenues for personalized, responsive, and scalable care through advances in predictive analytics, digital biomarkers, robotic systems, adaptive therapies, brain–computer interfaces, and digital monitoring tools. While early studies showcase AI’s potential to enhance rehabilitation outcomes and support clinicians in decision-making, ethical challenges are emerging as these technologies move from theoretical promise to widespread clinical implementation. In neurorehabilitation, where patients may have cognitive, communicative, or motor impairments and where long-term, multidisciplinary care is the norm, concerns arise over patient autonomy, privacy, fairness, and the preservation of dignity and quality of life. Despite significant technological trials and theoretical commentary, there remains a pressing need for robust, actionable frameworks that address ethical risks and practical questions f

title: Executive Function, Shared Intentionality, and Interbrain Synchrony: Cognitive, Embodied and Neural Mechanisms of Joint Attention
summary: In the field of cognitive science, understanding how humans coordinate thought and action with others is central to research on joint attention, shared intentionality, and executive function. Recent advances emphasize the interplay between high-level cognitive mechanisms and neural processes, particularly during real-time social interactions. Despite this progress, critical questions remain regarding the specific neural dynamics enabling shared goals, coordinated attention, and joint action: What are the cognitive and neural bases for linking executive function with shared intentionality? How do oscillatory brain activities support the mechanisms of joint attention, and how does interbrain synchrony reflect interpersonal coordination beyond shared perceptual input? What is the relation between the neural and embodied aspects of the dynamics of joint interaction? title: On the bridge of motor-cognition interaction and robots
summary: Human motor system executes the motor command from high-order regions, rigorously controls the musculoskeletal system and learns to adapt to novel stimuli of dynamic environments. Due to the highly redundant characteristics of the motor system, understanding the optimal and individualized principles of motor control and motor learning is still a scientific challenge. Understanding how brain controls motion and how musculoskeletal system performs commands from the brain and interacts with physical world is a focus for basic science, engineering and clinical translation.

title: Overcoming Resistance in Epilepsy: From Mechanisms to New Therapies
summary: Epilepsy remains one of the most common neurological disorders, yet approximately 30% of patients have drug-resistant (refractory) epilepsy, failing to achieve seizure control with current antiseizure medications (ASMs). This persistence underscores the critical need to shift focus from symptomatic seizure suppression to disease-modifying treatments and novel molecular targets.

title: Positive Equine Welfare
summary: Positive equine welfare is an emerging research area that shifts the focus from simply preventing suffering to actively promoting conditions in which horses can thrive. Traditionally, assessments of welfare centered on the absence of pain, injury, and disease, but current perspectives recognise that optimal welfare also depends on how horses feel, how they interact, and how well their environments meet their species-specific needs.
image_alt: Positive Equine Welfare

title: Reflective and self-regulating architectures in embodied and agentic AI systems
summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have enabled the development of embodied and agentic systems capable of operating in dynamic, real-world environments. While these systems exhibit increasing autonomy and performance, their underlying architectures remain largely focused on optimization, control, and task execution. Consequently, critical limitations persist, including limited awareness of uncertainty, the absence of robust self-monitoring mechanisms, insufficient decision traceability, and inadequate alignment with human values in high-stakes contexts.

title: Sensory processing dysregulation as a regulatory core in ASD, ADHD, and PTSD
summary: Sensory processing abnormalities are consistently observed in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), manifesting as patterns of hyper- and hypo-responsivity across auditory, tactile, visual, olfactory, and nociceptive domains. These abnormalities are typically treated as secondary features rather than mechanistic contributors to core dysfunction, limiting our understanding of how sensory encoding and filtering shape emotional regulation, attentional control, and reward-based behavior.
image_alt: Sensory processing dysregulation as a regulatory core in ASD, ADHD, and PTSD

title: Sex-dependent and lifespan-related variation in glial biology: From neurodevelopment to neurodegeneration
summary: Glial biology has evolved from viewing glia as passive support cells to understanding them as essential regulators of brain development, homeostasis, and disease. Microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and their progenitors orchestrate synaptic pruning, circuit refinement, and myelination while coordinating immune and metabolic balance and maintaining neurovascular integrity. When these processes are perturbed, glial dysfunction contributes to a cascade of changes underlying developmental, neurodegenerative, and neuropsychiatric disorders. Despite major progress, central questions persist about how glial diversity adapts during development, ageing, and disease, and to what extent biological sex shapes these processes.

title: The Trajectory of ADHD Across the Lifespan
summary: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a complex and highly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition. Historically, ADHD research and clinical practice have been heavily skewed toward childhood and early adolescence. However, contemporary evidence unequivocally demonstrates that ADHD is a lifespan condition. Its presentation, functional impact, and associated challenges evolve continuously from early childhood into adulthood, and increasingly, into older age.

title: Toward precision brain stimulation: mechanisms, methods, and applications
summary: The landscape of brain stimulation is evolving rapidly, with TMS, TES, TUS, DBS, and other emerging neuromodulation techniques increasingly integrated with neuroimaging and computational methods to enable more targeted and individualized interventions. These developments are expanding our capacity to probe, modulate, and quantify human brain function across multiple spatial and temporal scales, driving a shift from standardized protocols toward adaptive and personalized modulation of brain circuits that accounts for individual variability and dynamic brain states.

title: In the Shadow of Neurodevelopmental Processes and Media-Digitalism Impacts: The Evolution of Play from Unoccupied Play to Game Design
summary: Liberated from the rules, obligations, and pressures of daily life, yet standing at its very core, play promises absolute freedom and happiness not only to humans but also to animals. Allowing us to become both actor and spectator, play is perhaps the ultimate safe haven where we soothe our existential anxieties. The Vygotskian understanding of play constitutes a central context in which children develop abstract thinking and self-regulation, internalize speech through the transition from social to private and inner speech, and demonstrate their learning potential within the zone of proximal development. Concurrently, through a Piagetian lens, dramatic and imaginative forms of play serve as primary manifestations of cognitive growth, fostering early metacognitive awareness and nurturing the capacity to “think about thinking.” This Research Topic aims to generate actionable insights for early childhood education policies, game-based learning curricula, digital play environment designs,

title: Advances in Radiotherapy Dosimetry for Neuro-Oncology: From Film-Based Techniques to Emerging High-Precision Applications
summary: Accurate radiation dose delivery is fundamental to safe and effective radiotherapy, particularly in neuro-oncology, where treatments often involve small targets, steep dose gradients, and close proximity to highly radiosensitive critical structures. Even minor uncertainties in dose measurement can have significant clinical consequences, underscoring the importance of robust, high-precision dosimetry for brain tumours and intracranial metastases. The field of radiotherapy dosimetry continues to evolve rapidly, driven by the increasing complexity of treatment techniques and the growing demand for accurate verification of delivered dose. Film-based dosimetry, including established and next-generation radiochromic film technologies, has long played a central role in high-resolution dose verification. At the same time, advances in detector design, calibration methodologies, scanner protocols, and data analysis approaches are reshaping best practices across clinical dosimetry. While newer ge

title: Advancing Excellence in Multiple Sclerosis and Neuroimmunology: Breakthroughs and Impactful Discoveries
summary: The field of Neuroimmunology, and particularly research regarding Multiple Sclerosis (MS), has experienced rapid growth and unprecedented innovation over the past decade. This includes the discovery of cutting-edge biomarkers, the evolution of targeted therapeutic strategies and improvements in diagnostic pathways for MS and related neuroimmunological disorders.

title: Advancing Neurological Biomarkers for Prognosis and Recovery following Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) represents one of the most pressing challenges in contemporary neuroscience, bridging neurotrauma research with translational medicine and clinical care. It is characterized by a cascade of complex biological and physiological events that extend well beyond the initial mechanical insult, leading to secondary injuries involving neuroinflammation, glial activation, microvascular dysfunction, and behavioral disturbances. Although early discovery of biomarkers such as Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP) and Ubiquitin C-terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) has improved diagnosis, their predictive accuracy for long-term outcomes remains considerably limited. Recent advances in multi-omic profiling, extracellular vesicle analysis, and neurovascular coupling have shed light on new mechanisms linking acute injury to chronic neurodegeneration. However, key questions persist regarding how molecular signatures, stress-related responses, and neurological adaptations intera

title: Behavior Change in Climate-Impacted Environments
summary: Weather, climate variability, and extreme environmental conditions can influence when, where, and how people go about their daily behaviors. Heat, rainfall, smoke exposure, and other environmental stressors may disrupt physical activity, sleep, mobility, nutrition and diet, social and work routines, and broader health-related behaviors. At the same time, wearable devices, smartphones, and other digital health tools are creating new opportunities to measure these behavioral responses continuously and at scale.

title: Biodiversity and ecosystem functioning of global peatlands
summary: This collection focuses on the biodiversity of microorganisms, flora and fauna and their linkages to ecosystem functioning of global peatlands from the poles to the tropics and from coasts to alpine regions.

title: Biofilms and antimicrobial resistance in livestock pathogens: mechanisms, detection and control
summary: Biofilms play a crucial role in the persistence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in livestock production systems. Pathogens affecting cattle, swine, and poultry often form biofilms on animal tissues and farm environments, increasing their tolerance to antimicrobials and host defenses. Advances in genomics, transcriptomics, and imaging have deepened our understanding of the molecular basis of biofilm formation and its link to horizontal gene transfer and resistome dynamics.This Research Topic aims to gather studies exploring the mechanisms, detection, and control of biofilm-associated AMR in veterinary pathogens. Emphasis will be placed on innovative strategies such as phage therapy, anti-biofilm peptides, quorum-sensing inhibitors, and nanomaterials. By integrating microbiology, veterinary medicine, and biotechnology, this collection seeks to provide new insights and practical solutions to mitigate biofilm-mediated resistance and promote sustainable animal production.

title: Brain Organization and Behavioral Asymmetries: From Sensory Processing to Cognition Across Species
summary: The two hemispheres of the brain are neither structurally nor functionally symmetrical, and these asymmetries are often reflected in behavior. For more than a century, it was a common but mistaken belief that lateralization was unique to the human brain. However, it is now well established that hemispheric asymmetries are fundamental components of sensory, cognitive, and motor systems across vertebrates and many invertebrates. Behavioral measures such as motor preferences and perceptual biases provide valuable tools for investigating these processes, reflecting links between observable behavior and neural organization. Evidence across taxa also suggests that hemispheric asymmetries may confer evolutionary advantages by enhancing neural efficiency and supporting perceptual, cognitive, and motor performance, with potential benefits for survival.

title: Bridging Brain and Body: Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Exercise and Cognitive Health
summary: The relationship between physical activity and cognitive health has become an important focus in neuroscience, behavioral medicine, and health research. In the context of increasingly sedentary lifestyles and growing cognitive demands, understanding how the body influences the brain is more important than ever. A central concept in this field is neuroplasticity, as physical exercise may induce structural and functional changes in the brain that support cognitive function and resilience against aging and neurological decline.

Changes in the brain and neurovascular extracellular matrix (ECM) remain an understudied mechanism in the neurodegenerative process. title: Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI in neurological disorders
summary: Chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has rapidly emerged as a pivotal tool in neuroimaging, enabling the non-invasive quantification of molecular and metabolic processes in the brain. Unlike conventional anatomical MRI, which predominantly reflects structural integrity, CEST MRI probes the chemical interactions between water and endogenous metabolite protons, offering sensitivity to subtle biochemical alterations that precede overt morphological damage. This approach provides unique insights into early metabolic dysfunction and neurochemical changes in diverse neurological disorders. Recent advances in high and ultra-high field MRI technology have improved spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratios, facilitating more specific detection of protein and metabolite pools such as glutamate, creatine, and glucose. title: Climate change and its influence on aquatic parasite-host interactions
summary: Aquatic parasitology is undergoing significant transformation due to the pervasive effects of climate change on marine and freshwater environments. Global shifts in temperature, precipitation patterns, and chemical composition of water bodies are altering ecosystems, profoundly impacting the delicate balance between parasites and their aquatic hosts. Historically, the distribution, prevalence, and diversity of parasites were largely governed by relatively stable environmental parameters. Recent research, however, points to accelerating changes in disease emergence, shifts in parasite-host ranges, and unpredictable fluctuations in infection rates across fish, amphibians, and invertebrates. This evolving landscape has placed significant stress on biodiversity, fisheries productivity, and aquaculture sustainability, with broader repercussions for human health and ecosystem resilience.

This Research Topic aims to delve into the intricate co-evolutionary dynamics between social communication systems and the increasing complexity of social organization across the tree of life. We particularly welcome contributions that apply quantitative, computational, and network-based frameworks to illuminate these dynamics.

title: Embodied Intelligence for Soft Robots: Proprioception, Perception, Learning, and Control with Advanced Sensing and Actuation
summary: Recent advances in robotics are increasingly driven by the integration of intelligent algorithms, advanced sensing technologies, and novel actuation mechanisms. In particular, the emergence of soft robotics has introduced new opportunities for safe and adaptive interaction with complex environments, enabled by compliant materials and innovative actuation methods e.g., pneumatic actuators. At the same time, progress soft sensor technologies such as optoelectronic sensors has enhanced proprioception capabilities, while machine learning and model predictive control have improved decision-making and system performance. Despite these developments, unifying perception, perception, learning, and control across both rigid and soft robotic systems remains a significant challenge, especially under uncertainty and in dynamic real-world conditions.

title: Everyday Brain and Systemic Health Wearables: Validity and Equity
summary: Consumer-grade wearables systems incorporating electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and photoplethysmography (PPG) have moved rapidly from research laboratories into everyday life, offering the promise of continuous, passive monitoring of stress, sleep quality, and cognitive focus. Advances in miniaturization, wireless transmission, and machine learning have enabled the instrumentation of daily activities that were previously confined to controlled experimental settings. Yet, a widening gap persists between the conditions under which these devices are developed and validated and the complex, uncontrolled environments in which they are ultimately used. Motion artifacts, ambient noise, interindividual physiological variability, and the inherently lower signal fidelity of consumer hardware all challenge the direct translation of laboratory-grade metrics into meaningful, reliable readouts in daily life. Improving Vision-Guided Robotic Systems Through Next-Generation Hand-Eye Calibration Techniques
summary: Robotic vision systems form the foundation of modern industrial automation, enabling high-precision tasks such as assembly, inspection, and object manipulation. Central to their performance is hand-eye calibration, which defines the spatial relationship between the robotic manipulator and the visual sensor. Traditional calibration methods typically rely on multiple feature points, complex mathematical transformations, and iterative optimizations, increasing the risk of cumulative errors and computational inefficiencies. Recent approaches leveraging simplified configurations—such as single fixed feature point methods and algorithms like Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Levenberg-Marquardt (LM)—have shown promise in reducing setup complexity. However, persistent issues with accuracy, robustness to sensor noise, and adaptability to dynamic environments highlight the need for innovative solutions that balance precision with operational efficiency.

title: Innovation in Maxillary and Mandibular Fracture Repair and Maxillofacial Reconstruction in Small Animals
summary: This Research Topic aims to explore and clarify the clinical effectiveness, complication profiles, and cost–benefit aspects of minimally invasive and advanced maxillofacial surgical techniques in small animals. The goal is to develop validated, standardized outcomes and to construct informative decision-support tools that take into account patient-specific risks and practitioner experience. By addressing critical questions—such as whether minimally invasive or patient-specific approaches improve functional recovery and reduce complications relative to conventional techniques—and by evaluating how contemporary biomaterials influence healing, the Research Topic seeks to transform both everyday and advanced surgical management through a robust evidence foundation.

summary: Systems-level thinking has transformed how we study life across scales, from molecules and cells to populations, communities and whole ecosystems. The Integrative Systems Ecology, Evolution and Plant Science section sits at the meeting point of systems biology, ecology, plant science, environmental science, evolution and synthetic biology, with a particular focus on how organisms and ecosystems respond to climate change, global change and biodiversity loss. This collection celebrates that progress: it brings together leading voices to highlight state-of-the-art developments and to set the agenda for the questions that will define the field next. This Research Topic aims to provide an overview of the most recent advances in integrative systems ecology, evolution and plant science. Neuroendocrine and Neurochemical Mechanisms of Parental and Reproductive Behavior Across Species
summary: Parental and reproductive behaviors are expressed across diverse taxa, yet their hormonal regulation reflects both evolutionary conservation and species-specific adaptation. Comparative research demonstrates that neurotransmitters, neuropeptides, and steroid hormones modulate mating, bonding, nesting, incubation, lactation, and offspring defense in all vertebrates. Advances in molecular genetics, neuroimaging, and circuit-level manipulations have revealed conserved hypothalamic and limbic pathways that integrate hormonal and neurochemical signals with environmental and social cues. Interestingly, the behavioral expression of these neural systems varies dramatically across mating systems, life histories, and ecological niches. Ethologically grounded approaches, integrating natural behavioral observation with endocrine and neural measures, have been essential for revealing how hormonal mechanisms operate within real social and environmental contexts. title: Neuroprotection Strategies to Induce CNS Resilience and Functional Recovery
summary: Disorders of the central nervous system (CNS), including neurodegenerative, ischemic, neuroinflammatory, and traumatic conditions, remain leading causes of disability and cognitive decline worldwide. Despite major advances in understanding disease mechanisms, clinically effective neuroprotective therapies are still scarce. A central obstacle is translating mechanistic insights into actionable targets and therapeutic regimens that robustly activate endogenous protective programs, preserve neural circuit integrity, and sustain CNS homeostasis amid diverse stressors.

title: Nutritional neuroscience: How sensory signals influence diet and cognitive function
summary: Despite growing awareness of the role of nutrition in health and cognitive function, the intricate neural mechanisms linking sensory signals and dietary behavior remain underexplored. Sensory cues like taste, smell, and texture significantly influence food preferences, portion control, and satiety, yet how these signals interact with brain regions involved in reward, decision-making, and memory is not fully understood. This gap in knowledge limits our ability to develop effective interventions for nutritional challenges such as obesity, eating disorders, and age-related cognitive decline.

title: Pain as motivation: homeostatic regulation of behavior and decision-making
summary: Pain, homeostasis, and cognition function as an integrated system, which drives adaptive behavior. Pain is more than a sensory signal of injury; it is a motivational force that demands a decision to avoid, to escape, to tolerate, or to endure an aversive state. This decision is shaped by an organism’s flux of homeostatic condition regarding the organism’s emotional state, their cognitive resources, and their motivational priorities. Fundamentally, pain is a multidimensional phenomenon that encompasses sensory processes and identifies disruptions, including affective–motivational processes that assign salience and urgency and cognitive–evaluative processes that guide decisions (good or bad) based on associated experiences and the current context.

summary: This volume is a collection of essays and papers examining emerging themes relating to the interactions between people and the rest of nature in the ‘Anthropocene’. These themes are often driven by global change and typically manifested as changes to landscape. The consequences of long-term, intimate connections between people and place with people ‘a part of nature’ rather than ‘apart from nature’, are reflected in the Anthropocene through the eco-cultural nature of landscapes, derived from our long-term environmental history. Key areas of interaction include development of novel and recombinant ecologies and their associated management problems increasingly evidenced around globally. In the contemporary, rapidly changing Earth system, the breakdown of intimate connections between Local communities including Indigenous Peoples, and their immediate access to nature or natural resources can trigger the process of ‘cultural severance’. title: Phylodynamics for One Health surveillance: wastewater, metagenomics, and scalable Bayesian methods for multi-pathogen monitoring
summary: Phylodynamics, the discipline uniting evolutionary, epidemiological, and ecological inference from genomic data, is increasingly fundamental to One Health practice. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated its transformative capacity: near real-time reconstruction of pathogen evolution now supports outbreak response, variant tracking, and intervention design. Yet most analytical frameworks remain narrowly tailored to single-pathogen, clinic-derived datasets, while modern surveillance demands the simultaneous tracking of diverse pathogens across environmental reservoirs, hosts, and regions. Achieving this integration at the required scale confronts scientists with heterogeneous sequencing data and computational limitations that inhibit unified inference.

Understanding reading as a cognitive, cultural, emotional, and social experience is essential for assessing its contribution to health and, particularly, to mental well-being across the lifespan.

While contemporary research has explored the use of Extended Reality (XR) platforms to manage pain and distress, these interventions frequently adopt a standardized, non-individualized approach. As a result, their long-term therapeutic potential remains constrained, particularly in complex pediatric populations where emotional and social dimensions are deeply intertwined with physical health. title: From Crisis to Recovery: Biological Responses to Environmental Change in the Fossil Record
summary: The fossil record provides a unique archive of how life on Earth has responded to environmental and climatic perturbations through deep time. Marine ecosystems have repeatedly experienced episodes of rapid change, including thermal maxima, cooling events, ocean anoxia, salinity crises, and major basin reconfigurations. These perturbations often triggered profound ecological and evolutionary responses, ranging from shifts in species distributions and community composition to morphological innovations, changes in body size, calcification strategies, and patterns of endemism. By documenting these biological responses, the fossil record allows us to reconstruct how ecosystems adapted to, survived, or recovered from environmental stress. Such events not only shaped biodiversity through Earth’s history but also provide valuable natural experiments to understand the resilience and vulnerability of marine ecosystems.

title: Leading Through Transformation: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Employee Mental Health
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the nature of work, influencing organizational structures, job roles, and interpersonal dynamics. As AI systems become increasingly embedded in decision-making, performance assessment, and communication processes, they not only enhance productivity but also reshape the psychosocial environment where employees operate. While these technologies can improve efficiency and support well-being initiatives, they also introduce new challenges,heightened stress, uncertainty about job security, and diminished autonomy ,all of which are key determinants of mental health. These changes extend beyond individual workplaces to affect population well-being and public mental health at large. Yet, the current evidence base remains fragmented, with limited understanding of how AI integration impacts psychological outcomes and what leadership strategies most effectively protect mental health in digitally evolving workplaces.

summary: Mental and physical health have traditionally been investigated and managed within separate disciplines. However, growing evidence demonstrates that the brain and the heart function as a highly integrated and dynamic biological system connected through complex neural, autonomic, endocrine, immune, metabolic, inflammatory, behavioral, and psychosocial pathways. Rather than representing a simple anatomical or physiological connection, the Brain–Heart Axis may be viewed as an integrative framework influencing the prevention, development, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and long-term outcomes of mental disorders and a broad spectrum of chronic physical diseases.

Behavioral phenotyping still rests on clinical examination at the bedside, with standardized neurobehavioral rating scales detecting behavioral signs of consciousness with improved reliability and validity compared to clinical consensus alone. title: Rehabilitation Robotics: Clinical Effectiveness and Patient Engagement
summary: Medical robotics is entering a new phase of development, one in which technological innovation is increasingly expected to translate into meaningful benefits for patients’ recovery, participation, and overall wellbeing. In rehabilitation, robotic systems are no longer viewed only as tools for assistance or repetition, but as part of broader care pathways that can support motivation, autonomy, continuity, and personalized intervention. At the same time, patient engagement has become a central concern in the design and implementation of effective rehabilitation strategies. Advances in wearable and assistive robotics, soft systems, intelligent sensing, remote care, and digital health integration are creating new opportunities to connect physical rehabilitation with more responsive and patient-centered models of support. This Research Topic aims to explore that growing convergence and to highlight contributions that can shape the next generation of rehabilitation-oriented medical robotics.

title: Social Robotics and Artificial Intelligence for Inclusion: Assistive and Interactive Technologies
summary: Social robotics and artificial intelligence are emerging as powerful tools for promoting inclusion and accessibility for people with disabilities. Individuals with cognitive, motor, sensory, or multiple impairments continue to face barriers in education, communication, mobility, employment, and social participation. Advances in socially interactive robots, virtual agents, adaptive AI systems, and intelligent assistive technologies are creating new opportunities to address these challenges, support autonomy, and foster meaningful engagement in learning, care, and everyday activities. Such technologies can support communication, scaffold learning processes, and provide personalized assistance adapted to users’ needs and preferences. At the same time, the deployment of these systems raises important ethical, social, and cultural considerations when applied to vulnerable populations. This Research Topic invites contributions that examine how social robotics and AI can be responsibly design

title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS)
summary: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) arises from compression of the neurovascular structures passing through the thoracic outlet, and presents across a broad clinical spectrum — from classic neurogenic TOS involving brachial plexus compression, to vascular forms affecting the subclavian artery or vein, to the widely debated “disputed TOS” in which symptoms persist without objective neurological abnormalities. The absence of universally accepted diagnostic criteria has long fueled controversy between neurologists and surgeons, and remains one of the central challenges in managing this condition.
